detail.abstract: The AI-Powered Vaidya System represents a comprehensive digital platform designed to streamline and modernize clinic and hospital management operations. This web-based application addresses the critical challenges faced by small to medium-sized healthcare facilities in managing patient records, appointments, staff coordination, billing, and administrative workflows. Built using the Model-View-Controller (MVC) framework with Visual Studio as the integrated development environment, the system employs HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for front-end development, while SQL Server manages the backend database operations. The platform comprises seven core modules: Security and Authentication, Patient Management, Appointment Scheduling, Doctor and Staff Management, Prescription Generation, Billing, and Reporting. Each module is designed with role-based access control to ensure data security and operational efficiency. The system incorporates artificial intelligence capabilities to automate repetitive tasks, optimize appointment scheduling, enhance security through anomaly detection, and provide predictive analytics for decision-making. Developed on Windows 11 with a Ryzen 5 processor and 8GB RAM, the system is architected for scalability, allowing seamless integration of additional modules such as pharmacy management and inventory control. The platform facilitates real-time information access through web browsers, enabling healthcare professionals to deliver improved patient care while maintaining comprehensive digital records. Future enhancements include advanced AI-driven diagnostic support, mobile application development for on-the-go access, and telemedicine capabilities for virtual consultations and remote patient monitoring.

title: Behavioural Manipulation Index: A Pilot Framework for Quantifying Cognitive Bias in Loyalty Programs

detail.title: Behavioural Manipulation Index: A Pilot Framework for Quantifying Cognitive Bias in Loyalty Programs
detail.abstract: This report illustrates the pilot study of the Behavioural Manipulation Index (BMI), a conceptual framework created to assess the degree with which loyalty programs use cognitive biases. The BMI focuses on the five, biases: loss aversion, goal-gradient effects, sunk costs, decoy/complexity, and status quo inertia, and uses a structured coding system to identify and assess the degree to which these biases are present. The pilot examined 32 programs across airlines, hotels, retail, Food & Beverage (F&B), digital services, and subscriptions. The preliminary outcomes provide some evidence of a link between a higher BMI score and increases in customer retention. Some program features, such as expiring rewards, countdowns, and boiler plate difficulty in cancelling, illustrate how certain behavioural biases are intentionally built into the design of the loyalty programs. The pilot illustrates both the managerially efficacious use of loyalty programs as well as the ethical implications of the use of these programs, to inform future applied and theoretical research.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am serving as an expert witness in this proceeding on behalf of the CPUC's Public Advocate's Office. My testimony draws on my previous original research which was not funded by any party.

detail.abstract:
The CPUC has authority to condition approval of the proposed transaction on rules that limit the rates charged for broadband Internet access service at monopoly-served locations.

Rate regulation is a longstanding and lawful response to monopoly power in utility and communications markets. Longstanding economic theory and empirical evidence demonstrate that monopoly control over essential communications infrastructure results in higher prices, lower quality, economic harms by way of deadweight loss, and regressive transfers from consumers to providers. Policymakers have thus repeatedly adopted schemes of rate regulation to address these concerns while preserving incentives for investment and competition. The proposed merger condition follows this tradition by tethering the rates charged at monopoly-served locations to competitive benchmarks.

This condition is within the scope of the CPUC’s powers. Section 854 of the California Public Utilities Code requires both that the CPUC ensure that any merger-related cost efficiencies (if any at all) are equitably allocated among shareholders and ratepayers and that it preemptively address any foreseeable harms of consolidation. Likewise, § 706 of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 and California Public Utilities Code §§ 451, 701, and 728 empower the CPUC to regulate broadband rates when doing so would advance the public interest. The CPUC may impose this condition also to preserve competition in telephone service markets. See Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 216(a)(1), (b). No provision of federal law preempts or otherwise prohibits the CPUC from exercising these ratemaking authorities—to the contrary, recent federal decisions confirm that the states retain their traditional regulatory powers over broadband service, given the lack of federal power to regulate broadband markets.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of online learning platforms has created unprecedented access to educational resources; however, it has also introduced significant challenges related to content overload, inappropriate course selection, and low learner engagement. Learners frequently struggle to identify courses that align with their current skill levels, learning objectives, and career aspirations, resulting in inefficient learning paths and high dropout rates. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an artificial intelligence-based online learning recommendation system designed to personalize learning experiences through intelligent data-driven techniques. The proposed system analyzes diverse learner data, including demographic information, academic background, learning behavior, interaction history, and assessment performance. By applying machine learning and data analysis techniques, the system constructs comprehensive learner profiles and dynamically identifies individual skill gaps. Based on these insights, personalized course recommendations are generated to enhance learner engagement, improve learning efficiency, and support continuous skill development.

title: How Do Scholars Define ‘Big Tech’?
affiliations: , iHub, Radboud University, Nijmegen and Radboud University Nijmegen

detail.title: How Do Scholars Define ‘Big Tech’?
detail.abstract: The term 'Big Tech' has become central to academic, political, and media debates about power and dominance in the digital economy. Yet despite its diffusion, the term remains analytically unsettled, hindering cumulative research, obscuring comparative analysis, and complicating debates that would benefit from precision. This paper examines how scholars define Big Tech and assesses the conceptual coherence of the term. Drawing on a systematic review of 225 peerreviewed articles indexed in Scopus, we analyze both extensional definitions (lists of companies) and intensional definitions (naming characteristics). We find that most scholars use extensional definitions, but they use varying definitions. Across the corpus, scholars mention 134 different companies as examples of Big Tech. We show that definitional boundaries are partly shaped by scholars' geographic affiliations: authors with non-Western institutional ties use more non-Western companies in their definitions. Intensional definitions are less common and show much variety. We identify nine clusters of characteristics that scholars see as typical for Big Tech, including platform dynamics, conglomerate power, and behavioral strategies. We hope that in the future, scholars will clarify what they mean when they talk about Big Tech. Greater definitional transparency is necessary for cumulative research and fruitful debate.

title: SV-1.0: A Proprietary Framework for Systemic Debt Stabilization and Anti-Crisis Management in the Global Economy

detail.title: SV-1.0: A Proprietary Framework for Systemic Debt Stabilization and Anti-Crisis Management in the Global Economy

declarations.ethicsApproval: Moldova

detail.abstract: The global financial system faces an unprecedented challenge with total debt exceeding $318 trillion, driven by persistent structural imbalances where real interest rates exceed economic growth (r > g). Conventional macroprudential tools, including monetary easing and fiscal stimulus, have demonstrated diminishing returns and limited capacity to prevent systemic cascading defaults. This paper introduces SV-1.0, a proprietary systemic resilience framework designed to function as an automatic stabilizer for sovereign and corporate debt dynamics. Unlike traditional stress indicators, SV-1.0 integrates predictive indexing with actionable restructuring mechanisms, including multilateral netting, dynamic debt adjustment, and asset-backed conversion. Simulation results indicate that SV-1.0 can reduce effective debt burdens by 68-75% over a 10-year horizon, prevent $320-380 trillion in exponential debt growth, and reduce systemic crisis probability to less than 5%. Most critically, SV-1.0 provides crisis early warning signals 6-12 months in advance, outperforming all major financial stress indicators by a factor of 2-4 times in lead time. This paper analyzes the direct and indirect financial benefits for central banks, international trade, and national budgets, arguing that SV-1.0 offers a viable pathway to transform the global debt crisis from an existential threat into a manageable structural adjustment.

title: Reviews as Matchmakers: Dynamic Learning of Product Fit

detail.title: Reviews as Matchmakers: Dynamic Learning of Product Fit
detail.abstract: Consumer reviews are predominantly studied as quality signals-tools for sorting products from best to worst. But they also serve a routing function, helping consumers assess not whether a product is good but whether it is good for them. We model review text as a signal that different readers decode heterogeneously, generating personalized inferences without personalized delivery. As routing succeeds, the buyer pool homogenizes and the text signal degrades. The unique equilibrium features partial matching, sustained by a diversity dividend from mismatched consumers whose reviews cover features that fans' reviews miss. The binding constraint is the feature overlap between consumer types, which governs how much information a homogeneous review base can provide. The model generates implications for score-following, AI summaries that disproportionately harm minority types, and the interaction between reviews and algorithmic recommenders. An effective recommender degrades the review base by homogenizing the buyer pool, yet the two systems cover orthogonal dimensions, creating a tension platforms must manage.

title: Geopolitical Risk and Supply Chain Financing Bifurcation: Evidence from Global Semiconductor Manufacturing
affiliations: University of Cambridge, University of Cambridge and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk and Supply Chain Financing Bifurcation: Evidence from Global Semiconductor Manufacturing

declarations.funderStatement: Cambridge Trust

detail.abstract: Purpose: This study examines how geopolitical risk (GPR) influences the geographic configuration of supply chain financing in the global semiconductor manufacturing industry. Contrary to the prevailing "de-risking" narrative, we investigate whether GPR triggers a bifurcation pattern in investment flows. Design/methodology/approach: We analyze 3,738 semiconductor manufacturing deals from 2000 to 2025 using data from a premier startup and financing database, combined with the Caldara-Iacoviello Geopolitical Risk Index. Our identification strategy leverages temporal lag structures and the 2018 US-China trade war as a quasi-natural experiment. Findings: We find that elevated GPR is associated with increased, rather than decreased, Chinese semiconductor investment (H1: β = 0.0004, p = 0.031). The 2018 trade war accelerated this trend, with China's share rising from 7.6% to 34.6% (H2: β = 0.1147, p = 0.005). This increase in Chinese investment is negatively associated with US-allied economies' share, suggesting a zero-sum bifurcation (H3: β =-0.785, p < 0.001). We uncover significant heterogeneity within the allied bloc: while Western allies sharply reduced investment, Asian allies exhibited structural inertia consistent with a geopolitical distance decay effect, maintaining stable ties despite rising risks. Furthermore, the trade war amplifies the positive effect of GPR on Chinese investment (H4: β = 0.0012, p = 0.001). Originality: This study challenges the conventional "de-risking" narrative by demonstrating that geopolitical tensions catalyze domestic investment in strategic industries rather than capital flight. We introduce the concept of "supply chain financing bifurcation" to describe the dual divergence pattern in global semiconductor investment.

title: When Should Platforms Create Information Gaps? AI Summaries, Rating Alignment, and Demand Allocation

detail.title: When Should Platforms Create Information Gaps? AI Summaries, Rating Alignment, and Demand Allocation

publicationDetails.detailsText: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/401056870_When_Should_Platforms_Create_Information_Gaps_AI_Summaries_Rating_Alignment_and_Demand-Side_Efficiency

detail.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly deploy generative artificial intelligence to preprocess consumer reviews, yet it remains unclear how such technologies should be designed to improve demand allocation and operational efficiency in large-scale marketplaces. In particular, it remains unclear how AI-generated summaries interact with numerical ratings, the core operational signal platforms use to route demand across heterogeneous suppliers. This study examines how alternative configurations of AI-generated summaries influence the allocation of demand across suppliers. Using a large-scale randomized field experiment conducted with a major online platform in China, we show that AI-generated summaries function as an interface-level demand management mechanism whose effectiveness depends critically on the rating environment in which consumers operate. When summaries are misaligned with ratings, such as presenting pros and cons for highly rated merchants or emphasizing strengths for moderately rated ones, consumers expand their consideration sets and exhibit higher order incidence. Importantly, these effects are associated with a broader distribution of engagement across available options, as reflected in increased category level diversification. We further show that these effects are strongest in operational environments characterized by lower search costs and higher quality uncertainty, such as dense urban markets and large cities, but are significantly attenuated for standardized chain merchants. These findings suggest that AI-mediated interface design shapes how demand is formed and distributed across available supply without altering underlying supply characteristics. By conceptualizing AI-generated summaries as interface-level demand coordination mechanisms within multi-signal information systems, this study contributes to demand-side operations research by showing how platforms can use information design to structure the allocation of demand across heterogeneous supply.

title: Towards a Unified Framework for Social Bias in Humans and Algorithms
affiliations: and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Towards a Unified Framework for Social Bias in Humans and Algorithms
detail.abstract: Algorithmic decision-making systems now shape hiring, lending, health care, policing, education, and the flow of information online. Concerns about "algorithmic bias" have grown accordingly, but relevant research often remains siloed: social psychologists study categorization, stereotypes, and discrimination, while computer scientists study biased data, biased models, and formal fairness criteria. This chapter bridges the two literatures by treating algorithmic systems as artifacts of social cognition: the targets algorithms learn to predict are frequently the product of human judgments; models learn statistical regularities that mirror those judgments; and people then interpret and act on model outputs in discretionary ways. We organize this argument using the Algorithmic Cognition Cycle, a framework that traces bias across three linked stages-(1) biased human judgments and records (data generation), (2) bias in data representations and model predictions (model training), and (3) bias in how humans deploy, trust, and override algorithmic advice (human-algorithm decision making)-with feedback loops that can amplify disparities over time. Along the way we pair classic psychological mechanisms (e.g., social identity, stereotype content, motivated reasoning) with computational analogs (e.g., proxy labels, embeddings, fairness metrics, explainability tools), highlight limits of "purely technical" fixes in a persistently biased world, and offer actionable intervention points spanning data, models, interfaces, and governance. The goal is a shared vocabulary and a research roadmap that is maximally useful to graduate students working at the intersection of psychology and computer science.

title: Shareholder Voting Power
affiliations: Georgetown University Law Center

detail.title: Shareholder Voting Power
detail.abstract: This paper provides a quantitative analysis of shareholder voting power in U.S. public companies. I measure voting power as a shareholder's pivotality in all possible coalitions, isolating structural influence derived from share ownership while abstracting from realized voting behavior and proposal selection. Because exact pivotality calculations are tractable only for a limited number of shareholders, I develop a hybrid method that combines precise enumeration for the largest holders with approximations for remaining and unobserved shareholders, including retail investors. Empirically, voting power diverges sharply from voting weight: many shareholders with ownership stakes below 30 percent exhibit nearcomplete pivotality. Ownership concentration among other large shareholders is a key determinant of voting power. I then extend the framework to probabilistic voting environments and show how voting thresholds, retail support, and other large-shareholder support affect both decisiveness and the likelihood of prevailing. I apply these results to controlling shareholder doctrine, showing that corporate law's new ownership-based threshold fails to capture voting power.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: Studies that examine users’ perceptions of museum’s website quality are scarce. The purpouse of this paper is to propose a multi-group comparison between two superstar museums to outline the variables that define website quality regarding museum websites towards achieving e-loyalty, trust and perceived control.

Design/methodology/approach: The sample comprised 305 valid online questionnaires, collected from a panel survey using a quota-sampling technique. The proposed model was tested using partial least squares analysis multi-group comparison between Prado and Thyssen-Bornemisza museum websites.

Findings: Website quality plays a determinant role in users’ behavioural outcomes. As evidenced in the results for the first time in a museum setting, website quality has the potential of influencing e-loyalty, trust and perceived control. Besides, trust has a positive influence on e-loyalty and perceived control, on trust. The multi-group comparison revealed no significant differences between the two museum superstars, which offer highly useful insights for the correct design of these websites.

Originality/value: This research addresses a multi-group comparison using partial least squares, a quite recent technique that advances knowledge regarding this method. It contributes to knowledge museum website management and online literature by means of proposing website quality as a dimension that includes content, ease of understanding, emotion, informational fit-to-task, promotion and visual appeal and by revealing significant effects of the relationships of the proposed model. Museum managers are provided with valuable inputs to design websites in an appropriate and suitable way for their users so they will be more willing to repeat their navigation experience.

title: Tail Risk and Green Preferences: Impact of Distributional Assumptions on Environmentally-Adjusted Portfolios

detail.title: Tail Risk and Green Preferences: Impact of Distributional Assumptions on Environmentally-Adjusted Portfolios

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), Mission 4, Component 2, Investment 1.1. Specifically, Simone Giansante acknowledges financial support for the Project Title: 'A geo-localized data framework for managing climate risks and designing policies to support sustainable investments' (Cod id. 20229CWYXC, CUP: B53D23016710006). This project was part of the Call for tender PRIN 2022 No. 104 published on February 2, 2022, by the Italian Ministry of University and Research (MUR), and is funded by the European Union – NextGenerationEU.

detail.abstract: The integration of climate-related preferences into portfolio optimization is often constrained by the Gaussian assumption, which creates a methodological blind spot and may lead to systematic underpricing of the tail-risk exposure associated with carbon-intensive portfolios. By correcting this Gaussian bias through a non-parametric bootstrap approach, this study reframes sustainable investing as a robust strategy for enhancing financial resilience amid structural economic transitions. Within this framework, climate risk is modeled as an asymmetric volatility factor, capturing the non-linear "jump risks"-such as carbon tax shocks and abrupt regulatory changes-that drive the structural devaluation of brown assets. We augment a standard utility framework with an environmental preference parameter to demonstrate that distributional assumptions, rather than ethical preferences alone, critically shape the optimal green-brown allocation. Our findings show that the nonparametric approach leads to significantly more aggressive divestment from brown assets than Gaussian-based models, even when environmental preferences remain constant. This result suggests that a green portfolio tilt is not merely an ethical overlay but a quantifiable risk-management response to asymmetric transition risks. The implications are twofold. For investors, reducing exposure to carbon-intensive assets emerges as a fiduciary strategy for hedging transition-related shocks. For regulators, the results indicate that conventional stress-testing frameworks may substantially underestimate systemic climate-related financial fragility.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the household adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in the United States and Italy, leveraging survey data to compare usage patterns, demographic influences, and employment sectoral composition effects. Our findings reveal higher adoption rates in the US, driven by socio-demographic differences between the two countries. Despite their lower usage of GenAI, Italians are more confident in its potential to improve their well-being and financial situation. Both Italian and US users tend to trust GenAI tools less than human-operated services, but Italians report greater relative trust in government and institutions when handling personal data with GenAI tools.

title: The Effect of Pregnancy and Childbirth on Consumption Behavior
affiliations: Universidad Adolfo Ibanez, Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile and Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Marketing

detail.title: The Effect of Pregnancy and Childbirth on Consumption Behavior

publicationDetails.detailsText: Columbia Business School Research Paper(forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Major life transitions, such as pregnancy and childbirth, reshape lifestyles and purchasing priorities, yet causal evidence on how consumers reallocate spending across product categories remains limited. We quantify the effects of first-time parenthood by linking a large-scale transactional panel to verified birth records. To identify causal effects, we implement a difference-indifferences design augmented with causal forests, enabling flexible comparisons between households entering parenthood and carefully matched controls. We uncover a pronounced and dynamic behavioral trajectory. Spending and trip frequency decline early in pregnancy, rebound late in gestation, and increase sharply after childbirth. Post-childbirth, supermarket spending and ticket size rise by approximately 20-25%, accompanied by a 10% increase in promotional reliance and a systematic reallocation away from discretionary categories (e.g., dining, travel, beauty, pets) toward health-and family-oriented goods (e.g., fresh foods, yogurt, pharmacy items, baby products). Reduced leisure and personal-care spending is offset by higher expenditures on essential household categories, indicating lifestyle adaptation rather than uniform budget tightening. Heterogeneity is substantial: effects are larger among younger parents and households with higher baseline spending. These results identify childbirth as a major inflection point in consumer behavior and offer actionable guidance for retailers.

title: Climate Change and Alcohol Use: Evidence from US Retail Sales Data

detail.title: Climate Change and Alcohol Use: Evidence from US Retail Sales Data

publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the responses of alcohol sales to temperature shocks and evaluates how a warming climate influences alcohol sales across the United States. Using retail store sales data from 2006 to 2023 combined with product-level alcohol content from a barcode database, we convert weekly sales volume into ethanol-equivalent volume for each store. We find that alcohol sales, on average, rise with temperature up to roughly 90℉, beyond which the positive effect becomes smaller. The effect varies sharply by region: Warmer regions show much weaker responses to high temperatures than cooler regions, reflecting adaptation to hotter conditions. Applying these estimates to climate projections, national alcohol sales are projected to remain unchanged by mid-century under a high-emissions scenario, as increases in cooler regions offset declines in warmer regions. By the end of the century, sales are projected to decline by 2.4%, with larger declines in warmer regions (4.7%).

detail.abstract: Previous research documents persistent regional differences in national brand market shares, often attributed to geographic preferences and early entry advantages (Bronnenberg et al. 2007, 2009). This paper examines whether long-term vertical contracts help explain this persistence. Using NielsenIQ data from the same product categories as Bronnenberg et al. (2007), we decompose the variance in brand shares into Brand × Retailer and Brand × Market components following Abowd et al. (1999). Retailer effects explain about 50% of the variance, compared with 20% for market effects. These results suggest retailer-specific vertical contracts may play an important role in sustaining national brand dominance.

title: The Illusion of Oversight: Why Multiple Agencies Do Not Equal Accountability

detail.abstract: Modern healthcare oversight in the United States is structurally complex, involving federal agencies such as the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), the Office for Civil Rights (OCR), the Office of Inspector General (OIG), state licensing boards, accreditation bodies, and internal compliance departments. While this multiplicity suggests layered protection, fragmentation may paradoxically diffuse responsibility. This paper argues that overlapping jurisdiction across agencies can produce oversight paralysis rather than accountability. When escalation pathways become multi-directional and jurisdictionally siloed, responsibility may shift rather than resolve. Through regulatory analysis and comparative governance theory, this study conceptualizes fragmentation itself as a compliance vulnerability. Using a structural lens informed by administrative law and historical patterns of bureaucratic diffusion, the paper explores how systems designed to protect can unintentionally produce procedural silence. It proposes reforms aimed at jurisdictional clarity, coordinated review thresholds, and transparency in inter-agency referral processes. Oversight density does not necessarily produce accountability density. Without structural alignment, it may produce the illusion of oversight.

title: The Energy Barrier to Digital Immortality: A Physical and Philosophical Critique
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Energy Barrier to Digital Immortality: A Physical and Philosophical Critique
detail.abstract: The concept of digital immortality-the idea that human consciousness could be uploaded and preserved forever on digital substrates-has gained significant attention in technological and transhumanist circles. This paper argues that such aspirations face an insurmountable fundamental barrier: the finite nature of energy in a universe governed by thermodynamic laws. Through analysis of data center energy requirements, the impossibility of perpetual information maintenance, and the ultimate heat death of the universe, we demonstrate that digital immortality is physically impossible. The paper distinguishes between technologically possible "extended digital existence" and the true infinity implied by immortality, concluding that imagination, however beautiful, must ultimately submit to the strict laws of the cosmos.

title: Demographic Structure and International Capital Flows: Evidence from 140 Countries

detail.title: Demographic Structure and International Capital Flows: Evidence from 140 Countries
detail.abstract: We investigate the relationship between demographic structure and current account balances using the Fair-Dominguez polynomial age-distribution technique within the IMF's External Balance Assessment framework. Using data through 2024 from ten international sources across 140 countries-covering 97 percent of world population and 99 percent of world GDP-we estimate pooled GLS models with AR(1) correction. All three demographic polynomial variables are highly significant in the baseline model (all p < 0.001), with R-squared of 0.27 across 2,730 observations from 137 countries. However, a leave-one-region-out jackknife reveals moderate coefficient instability (CV approximately 30 percent), with the Central Asia and Caucasus group of 13 transition economies acting as the tipping point for statistical significance; these countries exhibit demographic slopes 3-8 times larger than the rest of the world, and direct testing rules out remittance dependence as the mechanism. Interactions between demographic polynomials and the Chinn-Ito financial openness index are jointly significant (p < 0.001), but a three-way interaction analysis reveals they operate exclusively through low-and middle-income countries (all p > 0.76 for high-income economies); a horse race against income-level interactions confirms this is genuinely about financial openness, not development level. In advanced economies, pension system generosity rather than financial openness mediates the demographic channel: demographic-pension interactions are jointly significant (p = 0.038 on EBA-49, all individual p < 0.008 on the full sample) and survive a horse race against KAOPEN interactions. The interest rate channel, insignificant through bank lending rates (p = 0.43), appears more clearly through government bond yields (p = 0.031) and term spreads (p < 0.001), though a two-stage test finds the demographics-to-yields first stage only suggestive (Z p-values 0.12-0.18). Projections through 2060 for 141 countries show that 92 economies currently face demographic headwinds, though the magnitude of projected effects scales linearly with the Z coefficients (CV approximately 30 percent across jackknife samples). A general equilibrium clearing rate overlay shows that the interest rate channel can absorb only 6-12 percent of peak GDP-weighted demographic surplus pressure, confirming that non-rate adjustment channels must bear the primary burden.

detail.abstract: Oppression of minority shareholders remains a persistent problem across many jurisdictions. Although corporate law in each jurisdiction has developed mechanisms to address this issue, no legal framework can yet be regarded as fully satisfactory. Against this backdrop, Professor Alan K. Koh’s Shareholder Protection in Close Corporations: Theory, Operation, and Application of Shareholder Withdrawal makes a timely and important contribution. Drawing on a sophisticated theoretical framework and extensive comparative analysis, the book advances a model withdrawal remedy that offers concrete and well-grounded guidance for legislators seeking to improve minority shareholder protection in close corporations.

title: Sufficient Statistics for Welfare with Unobserved Quality: Why Missing Sectional Demand Leads to First-order Errors
affiliations: Tohoku University - Graduate School of Information Sciences

detail.title: Sufficient Statistics for Welfare with Unobserved Quality: Why Missing Sectional Demand Leads to First-order Errors
detail.abstract: This paper provides a sufficient statistics approach to evaluate welfare changes under unobserved endogenous quality. We show that the "sectional" price elasticity, defined under completely fixed product quality, serves as a sufficient statistic for total surplus changes. While the classic framework by Spence (1975) focuses on the direct welfare effect of quality adjustment as a second-order "triangle", we show that overlooking quality rather leads to a first-order "rectangular" bias. This error arises because quality-driven demand shifts are mistaken for price-driven movements, resulting in a misidentified sectional elasticity. Using parameter estimates from Doi (2022) regarding the Japanese airline market, our numerical exercise reveals that this indirect bias is approximately six times larger than the direct Spencean effect, accounting for 60% of the total change in social surplus. These findings underscore a critical risk of policy misjudgment in today's digital economy, where rapid and pervasive quality adjustments by algorithms make the lack of "sectional" identification particularly fatal.

title: The Price of the Queue: Reinforcement Learning and the Cross-Section of Limit Order Values
affiliations: , Haas School of Business, University of California at Berkeley, University of California Berkeley, Haas School of Business, University of California Berkeley, Haas School of Business, Haas School of Business, University of California at Berkeley and Haas School of Business, University of California at Berkeley

detail.title: The Price of the Queue: Reinforcement Learning and the Cross-Section of Limit Order Values
detail.abstract: We apply a reinforcement learning framework to quantify the expected value of limit orders across twenty NASDAQ-listed equities spanning the full spectrum of tick-constraint regimes. Exploiting the uniform $0.01 tick size mandated by SEC Rule 612, we construct a natural experiment in which cross-sectional variation in the effective tick constraint arises purely from differences in natural spread width-free of the confounding variation in tick structures present in prior work on Australian markets. Our Q-learning estimates reveal a factor-of-eighteen range in best-bid order value, from-0.023 ticks for Amazon to +0.491 ticks for CrowdStrike, and uncover three novel empirical patterns. First, the price-level gradient inverts for tick-constrained stocks: orders placed two ticks behind the best bid carry higher expected value than orders at the BBO, reflecting the concentration of adverse selection at the top of the book. Second, the cancel option embedded in every limit order exhibits a universal intraday U-shape-peaking at market open and close across all twenty stocks and all four microstructure regimes-while the price-level gradient itself rotates from negative to positive over the trading day. Third, cross-stock policy transfer succeeds within microstructure clusters but fails catastrophically across them, with the absolute difference in log spread serving as a sufficient statistic for transfer regret (R 2 = 0.22). A state-by-state backtest validates these findings out of model: the RL policy outperforms all naive strategies in 20 of 20 stocks and beats the best economically-motivated heuristic in 17 of 20, with theoretical option values predicting realized performance gains at r = 0.72.

title: Estimating Parameters of Agent-Based Models from Data: A Methodological Review
affiliations: CENTAI Institute and CENTAI Institute

detail.title: Estimating Parameters of Agent-Based Models from Data: A Methodological Review
detail.abstract: Calibrating Agent-Based Models (ABMs) is essential for grounding their simulated dynamics in empirical reality, yet parameter estimation, a core part of calibration, remains a significant methodological challenge. In this review, we synthesize the diverse approaches developed across disciplines into a unified framework for ABM parameter estimation. We classify existing methods into three broad families---sampling-based, meta-modeling, and open-box approaches---and show that each ultimately tackles one or more of three fundamental tasks: (i) defining an appropriate loss function, including the selection of informative summary statistics and distance measures; (ii) computing this loss function efficiently despite the high computational cost of simulations; and (iii) optimizing it within a high-dimensional, nonlinear, and often non-differentiable parameter space. We highlight how methodological progress in simulation-based inference and probabilistic machine learning has shaped recent advances in ABM estimation, and we identify common pitfalls that hinder its reliability. Building on this synthesis, we provide practical guidance for choosing among existing methodologies and outline key research directions for developing robust data-driven ABMs. This review serves both as an entry point for researchers designing new inference methods and as a decision aid for practitioners seeking to calibrate ABMs in applied settings.

title: AML Obligations for Non-Custodial Crypto Wallets: A Functional Comparison of MiCA and U.S. Law
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: AML Obligations for Non-Custodial Crypto Wallets: A Functional Comparison of MiCA and U.S. Law
detail.abstract: The rapid growth of non-custodial cryptocurrency wallets has intensified regulatory debates concerning the scope of anti-money laundering ("AML") obligations applicable to decentralized financial infrastructure. Unlike custodial service providers, non-custodial wallet developers do not hold user assets, control private keys, or execute transactions on behalf of users, raising fundamental questions about the applicability of traditional intermediary-based AML frameworks. This article provides a comparative legal analysis of the regulatory treatment of non-custodial wallets under the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation ("MiCA") and the United States' functional AML framework as developed through FinCEN guidance and money transmission jurisprudence. It examines how both jurisdictions distinguish between regulated financial intermediaries and software-based providers, and identifies the functional thresholds at which AML obligations may be triggered in practice. The article argues that, in both the EU and the United States, non-custodial wallets generally fall outside the direct AML regulatory perimeter due to the absence of custody, control, and transaction execution. However, it demonstrates that AML exposure increasingly arises indirectly through interactions with regulated entities, including exchanges, fiat on-and off-ramps, and financial institutions. The analysis concludes that governance-based compliance frameworks-focused on transparency, role clarity, and partner risk management-represent a more proportionate and legally defensible approach for non-custodial wallet providers than transaction-level monitoring or customer due diligence obligations that they are structurally unable to perform.

title: Indian Constitution and Sustainable Economic Development: A Doctrinal and Jurisprudential Analysis
affiliations: Late. Mansaramji Padole Arts College Ganeshapur Bhandara

detail.title: Indian Constitution and Sustainable Economic Development: A Doctrinal and Jurisprudential Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Systems Engineering and Electronics (ISSN NO: 1671-1793) Volume 36 ISSUE 2 2026

detail.abstract: Background and Purpose: Adopted in 1950, the Indian Constitution includes provisions that create a basis for economic development that is sustainable. This predates modern conversations about sustainable development at the global level. This study asks: Which parts of the Constitution back sustainable development? How do these parts fit with today's ideas about sustainable development and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)? Methodology: This study uses legal research methods, looking closely at the words of the Constitution and at how the Supreme Court has interpreted it. It also compares these to the UN Sustainable Development Goals. The Constitution, amendments, Supreme Court decisions, and global development plans are the main sources. Books and articles on constitutional law, environmental law, and sustainable development are used as supporting sources. Key Findings: The Indian Constitution promotes sustainable development in several ways. It does this through Fundamental Rights (especially the right to life in Article 21), Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 38-51), Fundamental Duties (Article 51A(g)), and by setting up groups that promote shared governance (through the 73rd and 74th Amendments). Indian courts have also expanded environmental protections under the Constitution, creating ideas like the Polluter Pays Principle and the Precautionary Principle. The Constitution is in line with 13 of the 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals. Conclusions: The Indian Constitution offers a solid, legally supported plan for sustainable development. This plan came before and exists alongside global talk about sustainable development. By bringing together economic fairness, environmental care, and shared governance, the Constitution shows that true sustainable development needs to focus on fair distribution, environmental health, and democratic involvement all at once. India's experience with its Constitution gives helpful lessons for other countries that want to include sustainable development in their own constitutions.

title: The Lifecycle of Judicial Bias
affiliations: and Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS)

detail.title: The Lifecycle of Judicial Bias
detail.abstract: How does judicial bias arise and persist in the legal system? We trace the lifecycle of judicial bias in India's criminal courts, leveraging the quasi-random assignment of judges to courts and cases. We first document substantial variation in bias: within the same court, assigning a same-religion defendant from a judge at the 25th to 75th percentile of bias increases acquittal probability by 7.5 percentage points, 45% of the mean acquittal rate. We then examine how different triggers across judges' professional careers affect their bias. Exposure to Hindu-Muslim communal riots during a judge's first five years of service leads them to increase same-religion acquittal rates by 17.5%. Yet, judges who work alongside colleagues from different-religions during this critical period show no such effect. Next, social interactions between judges reinforce judicial bias. On-the-job exposure to biased colleagues leads judges to reduce acquittal rates for defendants of different-religions by 3.2 percentage points, with effects that persist for over a year. These findings suggest that judicial bias is neither innate nor inevitable, but rather shaped by experiences and relationships, and that thoughtful institutional design can prevent and mitigate discriminatory practices across various professions.

detail.abstract: This study compares the extent of informed trading across investor types in the Korean stock market using intraday quote and trade data. We estimate for each stock the probability of information-based trading (PIN) using trades that are initiated by foreign investors, domestic institutional investors, and local individual investors separately. The results show that the PIN values of foreign and domestic institutional investors are much higher than those of individual investors. Contrary to the belief of some market participants, however, we find that local institutional investors engage in more informed trading than foreign institutional investors.

title: AI, Productivity, and Labor Markets: A Review of the Empirical Evidence
affiliations: and International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE)

detail.title: AI, Productivity, and Labor Markets: A Review of the Empirical Evidence
detail.abstract: This issue brief reviews the empirical literature regarding the economic impact of generative AI through 2025. The authors discuss the “jagged frontier” of performance: while AI significantly boosts productivity in specific tasks like coding, writing, and customer service—often by 15% to 50%—these gains are most pronounced for lower-skilled workers, leading to “skill compression.” Despite fears of mass unemployment, aggregate data show limited labor-market disruption. Instead of widespread job loss, the evidence suggests a shift in “entry-level” roles, where AI automates tasks typically assigned to junior staff. Macroeconomic growth remains difficult to measure due to the “productivity J-curve,” in which firms must first invest in organizational changes before realizing financial gains. The authors conclude that because AI lowers entry costs for startups, policymakers should favor “strategic forbearance”—applying existing laws rather than creating new regulations that could stifle innovation and diffusion.

title: Robin Hood in a Field Experiment: Moral Framing, Discontent with Big Business, and Consumer Behavior
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong, Peking University - Guanghua School of Management, , The University of Hong Kong and Hong Kong Polytechnic University - Faculty of Business

detail.title: Robin Hood in a Field Experiment: Moral Framing, Discontent with Big Business, and Consumer Behavior
detail.abstract: We investigate how framing-based information about a large corporation shapes anticorporate behavior in a large-scale real-effort field experiment with a Fortune 500 firm and about 77,000 customers. Participants were offered a low-value coupon that required substantial effort to claim, making participation economically unattractive. Participation varied sharply with how we framed the sponsoring firm and the claiming act: labeling the sponsor as a large corporation and framing claiming as an opportunity to extract resources at its expense nearly doubled participation relative to a small-corporation label, with even larger effects when the firm's wage premiums were highlighted. We also allowed participants to forward the coupon to others, and forwarding behavior exhibited similar patterns. Survey evidence shows that our information treatments provoke discontent toward big business, indicating that anti-corporate sentiment can be manipulated through moral framing and slanted information.

title: Efficiency and Equity in an Experimental Repeated Entry Game
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Rady School of Management, INSEAD, Fundación Instituto de Empresa, S.L. - IE Business School and UCD, Michael Smurfit Graduate Business School

detail.title: Efficiency and Equity in an Experimental Repeated Entry Game

declarations.funderStatement: The study was funded by Grant PID2019-111512RBI00 from the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation and RMS Grant R21836 from the UCD College of Business.

detail.abstract: Motivated by the prevalence of competitive environments in which the same set of players face recurring entry decisions against one another, we experimentally study efficiency and equity in a repeated entry game. Analyzing 16,352 decisions from 511 subjects in 73 repeated entry games, we vary the prize structure (winner-take-all versus proportional), ability heterogeneity, the salience of performance feedback, and the availability of communication. Entry remains persistently above the efficient benchmark across all treatments, indicating that repetition alone does not eliminate it. A proportional prize lowers inequity but does not increase efficiency or reduce excess entry. Heterogeneous abilities improve efficiency but fail to reduce excess entry and worsen inequity. In contrast, providing a channel to communicate and salient feedback substantially reduces excess entry, improves efficiency, and produces more equitable outcomes. These joint gains arise because communication decreases the likelihood of momentum strategies, whereby early winners persistently re-enter, and facilitates coordinated turn-taking in which participants alternate entry over time. Our findings suggest that lightweight informational and communicative interventions can outperform structural incentive changes in improving long-run outcomes in repeated competitive environments.

title: Market Entrance, Patents, and Preliminary Injunctions: A Model of Pharmaceutical Patent Litigation
affiliations: and Copenhagen Business School

detail.title: Market Entrance, Patents, and Preliminary Injunctions: A Model of Pharmaceutical Patent Litigation
detail.abstract: The Patent Holder wishing to enforce her patent has several ways of doing so. In the world of patent litigation, however, one of the most important remedies is the preliminary injunction (PI), whereby an allegedly infringing competitor is forced to stop selling the goods in the market in the interim period before the court reaches its final decision on the merits. In spite of this, the economic literature has afforded little attention to PIs. This article uses a simple economic model to investigate how a Patent Holder and an Alleged Infringer will behave with and without the PI instrument. We show that party behavior depends on the probability that the Patent Holder does indeed have a valid patent and will prevail in a final court decision and on the extent to which courts can determine damages correctly. We find that while patent rights benefit the Patent Holder, the PI instrument to a large extent benefits the Alleged Infringer. It does so by insuring him against large damages payments and allowing him to receive compensation for actions not taken, i.e. for not being on the market in the interim period before the final court decision. Finally, we discuss different decision rules a court could use to decide whether to grant a PI, and propose a decision rule whereby courts can take into account the social benefits or losses of an erroneous PI decision.

title: Does News Trading Crowd Out Value Trading? Evidence from a Structural Estimation
affiliations: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

detail.title: Does News Trading Crowd Out Value Trading? Evidence from a Structural Estimation

declarations.funderStatement: Albert is grateful for financial support from the Dutch Research Council (NWO) for grant number 016.Vici.185.068.

detail.abstract: Technology produces data streams at lower cost, which intensifies "news" trading. Does this trading on value changes crowd out trading on value levels, i.e., value trading? And, what is the net effect on liquidity and market efficiency? We propose a Kyle (1985)-type model to study these questions, both theoretically and empirically. The latter is possible, because closed-form solutions admit structural estimation. Implementing it on a 2013-2023 proprietary sample covering trades in the EURO STOXX 50 Index Futures reveals how liquidity, market efficiency, and the profit of both types of informed trading changed over time, and why.

title: Using Patent Valuation Methods to Assess Damages in Patent Infringement cases Under the Unified Patent Court
affiliations: and University of Oxford

detail.title: Using Patent Valuation Methods to Assess Damages in Patent Infringement cases Under the Unified Patent Court
detail.abstract: We illustrate how publicly sanctioned IP valuation guidelines prevailing in Europe can be applied to assess damages as foreseen under the provisions of the UPC Agreement. With the help of a hypothetical example, we then evaluate if and to what extent the various ways proposed by European institutions to value IP fit with the provisions of the UPCA. We find that in situations where courts have all the necessary information required to determine damages, the IP valuation methods are a very useful tool in determining damages. It can however be expensive to obtain the necessary data to adequately determine damages.

detail.abstract: Tax havens exemplify the structural vulnerabilities of the international commercial order. They reveal how the nonapplication of coherent regulatory mechanisms between tax, trade and regulatory regimes has led to the existing state of affairs of fiscal sovereignty and global interdependence as they currently exist. This article argues that the existence of tax havens is not a mere fiscal anomaly, but rather the symptom of a deeper crisis of law and institutions in the fragmentation of international trade governance. By linking fiscal fragmentation with the legal fragmentation of law, the paper shows how the same forces which have brought about offshore financial regimes regulatory competition, insecure enforcement, and asymmetrical institutional power now return in the governance of digital and sustainable trade. Through a doctrinal and comparative analysis of regimes of tax, trade and environmental law, the paper identifies a parallel between the collapse of coherence of global tax law and the growing divergence between the WTO and the EU. It is concluded that in viewing tax havens as an early warning of systemic incoherence, the potential to inform the design of a new Legal Alignment Model for the reconciliation of multilateral and regional norms of trade law. The paper thus offers a new view of coherence as a preventive principle in international economic law.

title: Estimating Euler Equations with Measurement Error: A Nonparametric Approach
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Estimating Euler Equations with Measurement Error: A Nonparametric Approach
detail.abstract: This paper proposes two new identification schemes for estimating the parameter of intertemporal allocation, exploiting the equilibrium condition delivered by the rational expectations consumption model. The two identification schemes constitute an alternative to the existing methods of estimating Euler equations in the presence of measurement error. The small sample performance of the proposed identification schemes as well as that of existing approaches are evaluated by way of a MonteCarlo experiment.

title: Mergers and R&D Investment: A Unified Approach
affiliations: VU University Amsterdam and VU University Amsterdam - Department of Economics

detail.title: Mergers and R&D Investment: A Unified Approach
detail.abstract: We investigate the impact of mergers on R&D incentives within a framework of R&D competition where effort can influence both the probability of innovation and the payoff conditional on success. Our framework nests the results of two classes of existing models and reveals assumptions that are restrictive. In models where R&D effort increases the probability of innovation but does not directly affect the payoff upon success, we show that the assumption of zero payoff upon innovation failure is restrictive. In models where R&D effort influences the payoff conditional on success, but not the probability of success itself, the assumption of deterministic innovation success (i.e., a success probability of one) is similarly restrictive. Across both modeling approaches, we offer a novel insight: the shape of investment costs, and by implication the pre-merger level of innovation, can be pivotal in determining whether a merger strengthens or weakens firms' incentives to invest in R&D. In an extensions section, we further examine the role of R&D input and output synergies, firm asymmetries, as well as the implications for consumer surplus.

title: Sticking to Their Guns: Short-Horizon Exchange Rate Expectations
affiliations: University of Washington and London School of Economics

detail.title: Sticking to Their Guns: Short-Horizon Exchange Rate Expectations
detail.abstract: Short-horizon exchange rate forecasts systematically (and incorrectly) predict a partial reversal of their previous errors, both in consensus measures and forecaster-by-forecaster. This simple pattern spans almost 40% of the total variation in individual forecasts and explains their poor predictive performance at short horizons. We decompose short-term forecasts into three distinct components: (i) a component aligned with long-term forecasts, (ii) a component loading on the past error, and (iii) a residual component. The first two components account for three-quarters of forecast variance and--individually and jointly--predict exchange rate realizations. However, the second component predicts with a negative sign, offsetting the strong performance of the first component in the overall forecast.

title: In Search of Sparsity: Bayesian Sparse Factor Models and the Factor Zoo
affiliations: Government of Canada - Bank of Canada, CUNEF Universidad and Indiana University - Kelley School of Business

detail.title: In Search of Sparsity: Bayesian Sparse Factor Models and the Factor Zoo
detail.abstract: We develop a Bayesian Sparse Factor Model for asset pricing in factor zoo environments with correlated and weak factors. Observed factors are modeled as noisy measurements of latent priced risks, with hierarchical spike-and-slab priors on loadings to induce sparsity and quantify uncertainty about the factor structure. We embed the extracted factors in a Bayesian two-pass pricing framework that delivers inference on risk premia, pricing errors, and the implied stochastic discount factor (SDF). Empirically, three sparse latent factors summarize the zoo, remain competitive on the BHJ benchmark test sets, and produce tighter posteriors and a more stable SDF.

title: European Union's AI Act: Protecting the Public at the Cost of Innovation?
affiliations: Universidad de Chile, Arizona State University and

detail.title: European Union's AI Act: Protecting the Public at the Cost of Innovation?
detail.abstract: The Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) was adopted by the European Union (EU) in 2024, marking the first major regulation on AI. In this study, we analyze market reactions to cost-increasing and cost-decreasing events that preceded the Act's adoption, where cost-increasing (decreasing) events denote stricter (more lenient) regulation of AI but higher (lower) potential public trust benefits. We also investigate how country-level AI features and company characteristics moderate market reactions to these events. We find that the EU-wide market reaction to cost-increasing events is significantly negative and more pronounced in EU jurisdictions with high AI investment. Company-specific factors also moderate the market response. Larger companies experience positive abnormal returns on cost-increasing events, raising concerns that smaller firms may face a disproportionate regulatory burden (limiting competition for large companies). R&D spending is negatively associated with abnormal returns for cost-increasing events, particularly among companies operating in jurisdictions with high AI investment and industries expected to be affected by the regulation. These results suggest that EU investors expect higher costs and slower innovation following the AI Act. Rather than enhancing EU firms' competitive edge, the Act could widen the gap between the EU and its global AI competitors. This study is the first to examine market reactions to the AI Act, a landmark AI regulation.

title: Atemporal Structure of Monetary Units
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Atemporal Structure of Monetary Units
detail.abstract:
This study theoretically investigates the structural tension inherent in the functional definition of classical money under conditions of dynamic economic growth. Mainstream economics assumes that money simultaneously and perfectly performs its three functions — measure of value, medium of exchange, and store of value — but this paper argues that such a configuration constitutes a special solution that is only valid in a static model with fixed total factor productivity.

The object of this inquiry is not the practical efficiency of money's actual operation, but a more fundamental question: when economic theory presupposes the monetary unit as a 'time-invariant scalar,' can the formal conditions for that presupposition hold in a dynamic economy? This study argues that the essence of the problem lies in a structure in which no temporal dimension is embedded within the monetary unit — what this paper terms the 'Absence of a Temporal Axis.'

To this end, money is redefined as a 'future claim for intertemporal exchange,' and Lancaster's (1966) characteristics theory is extended to model the qualitative heterogeneity of goods as a vector z(t). The valuation function V(z(t)) = P(t) is axiomatically defined. After explicitly establishing the normative condition for the measure-of-value function — the condition that nominal prices must be monotonically proportional to productivity — this study mathematically proves that the store-of-value function and the measure-of-value function of money are necessarily in a trade-off relationship in an economy where productivity continuously improves through technological progress.

This trade-off is the logical consequence of the scalar structure in which the monetary unit does not embed a temporal dimension. In conclusion, this study argues that this structural tension is a theoretical necessity that holds in any dynamic economy in general, not a flaw of a specific institutional arrangement, and proposes the possibility of a new theory of monetary units that internalizes a temporal axis as a theoretical agenda.

title: Litigating Human Rights Harm in Global Value Chains: Evolving Pathways to Corporate Accountability
affiliations: University of Essex School of Law and Human Rights Centre and Independent

detail.title: Litigating Human Rights Harm in Global Value Chains: Evolving Pathways to Corporate Accountability
detail.abstract: Litigation seeking corporate accountability for human rights harms has mostly targeted parent companies for adverse impacts by their subsidiaries. Although human rights abuses in global value chains (GVCs) have long been on the business and human rights agenda, legal action has focused mainly on parentsubsidiary relationships rather than buyer-supplier dynamics. Despite obstacles to establishing parent company liability, this route has proven more viable due to closer relationships within corporate groups. By contrast, the ostensibly arm's-length, transactional nature of GVC relations has fostered reluctance to hold buyers liable for harms arising from their suppliers' operations, even when the former exert significant influence or leverage over the latter. Nonetheless, principles from parent-subsidiary litigation have created new possibilities for GVC litigation, which are now being tested before courts. This chapter explores the potential and limits of litigation for corporate accountability in GVCs. It traces this litigation trend in business and human rights, surveying key causes of action in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, and France. It evaluates the impact of human rights due diligence legislationespecially the French Law on the Corporate Duty of Vigilance-on future GVC claims.

title: Credit Growth and GDP Growth: A Cross-Country Measurement of Co-Movement

detail.title: Credit Growth and GDP Growth: A Cross-Country Measurement of Co-Movement
detail.abstract: How does credit growth co-move with GDP growth across countries and time horizons? This paper constructs a country-by-year panel of the credit-GDP co-movement ratio ω = Δlog(Y)/Δlog(M) for 43 countries over up to 79 years using BIS Total Credit Statistics. Two measurement contributions emerge. First, credit-GDP co-movement exhibits a frequency gradient: the Jordà LP coefficient rises from 0.54 (annual) to 0.83 (10-year), and from 0.19 to 0.47 in CPI-deflated real terms. The gradient survives wild cluster bootstrap inference and is not an artifact of co-trending. Second, crosscountry dispersion in ω far exceeds what independent or cointegrated trending would produce (empirical SD = 0.39 vs. mixed-null SD = 0.20, p < 0.001), revealing genuine heterogeneity in how economies convert credit into output. Advanced economies show particularly low annual co-movement (mean 0.13), consistent with large non-GDP credit sectors. A pre-/post-1971 regime difference (nominal Δω =-0.52) vanishes entirely under CPI deflation (Δω_real =-0.03, p = 0.80), indicating an inflation-regime effect rather than a structural change. The co-movement ratio ω carries no structural or causal interpretation; it is a descriptive statistic that complements the credit-to-GDP ratio by capturing growth-rate dynamics invisible in levels.

detail.abstract: We present a novel framework for predicting stock market crashes by analyzing structural properties of news articles rather than their sentiment. Our core hypothesis is that seemingly unrelated events accumulate structural characteristics such as information asymmetry, policy-reality gaps, and structural instability propagation that reach critical thresholds before market crashes. Using 20 years of KOSPI (Korea Composite Stock Price Index) data and 46.5 million news articles from the BigKinds database, we construct an end-to-end pipeline that: (1) extracts structural properties from news through unsupervised LLM-based generation with strict zero-bias protocols, (2) identifies statistically significant pre-crash patterns via temporal frequency analysis with FDR correction, and (3) builds a weighted risk scoring model. Our model achieves a test AUC of 0.907 with perfect precision (1.0) and 57.8% recall at zero false positive rate, notably outperforming its training-period performance (AUC 0.69), suggesting that structural patterns have become more pronounced in recent years. Further trajectory-based clustering analysis reveals two distinct crash types: structurally accumulated crashes (70/141, 49.6%) that the model can detect, and non-structural external shock crashes that are inherently unpredictable from news structure alone. This distinction itself constitutes a methodological contribution, refining the boundary of what news-based crash prediction can and cannot achieve.

detail.abstract:
Financial markets have traditionally relied on a single observable: the spot price. Yet spot prices are noisy, regime-dependent, and statistically unstable, making them extremely difficult to model within classical stochastic frameworks. 

This paper introduces a second, structurally determined fundamental: the geometric price, defined by the geodesic trajectory of the covariance manifold Sym + (17). This high-dimensional representation integrates the 11 GICS sectors, Gold, Crude Oil, the VIX, and key macroeconomic indicators. 

Unlike the spot price, the geometric price is neither an average nor a smoothed estimate; it is the deterministic equilibrium path dictated by the intrinsic curvature of the market. We establish the Two-Price Theory of Markets, wherein price dynamics arise from the interaction between the observable spot projection and the underlying geometric necessity. Their divergence defines Residual Stress, a measurable physical quantity that captures the tension between observed and structural states. Residual Stress admits a natural theoretical classification into compression, rupture, and suture regimes. 

While URF-3 provides the full geometric model for these regimes, their empirical computation requires complete spot-geodesic trajectories and will be delivered through the Econosysmographe as a Premium diagnostic module. Our empirical evaluation, based on a seven-window walk-forward audit using eight years of data (2018-2025), demonstrates strong structural congruence between spot and geometric prices. Sector ETFs, Gold, and long-duration Treasuries exhibit high directional accuracy (86-99%) and stable geometric inertia. Volatile assets such as Crude Oil and the VIX display curvature-breaking behavior, consistent with the theoretical predictions of the Two-Price framework. 

These findings challenge the Martingale paradigm by revealing that price formation is governed by deterministic geometric forces encoded in the covariance structure. URF-3 provides the foundational metrology for a new financial infrastructure and prepares the transition to URF-4, where the manifold acquires a Lorentzian signature, introducing causal structure and finite propagation speed into price dynamics.

title: Government Involvement in a Mandated Insurance Market: The Case of Workers' Compensation Insurance
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Government Involvement in a Mandated Insurance Market: The Case of Workers' Compensation Insurance
detail.abstract: I exploit the formation in the 1990s of state entities that provide health and disability insurance for work-related injuries and illnesses (workers' compensation) in competition with the private market. We can think of these entities as "public options," similar to those discussed in health care. By investigating the effects of these formations on insurer competition and underwriting performance, I offer insight on the debate about the merits of public options. I find that the introduction of public options increased market concentration overall, with public options gaining significant market share. Aggregate underwriting profitability appears to improve following the formation of public options, but this was largely driven by cuts in legislated benefit levels, rather than the public options themselves. I also document that the public options tend to charge higher prices, which may help to achieve the goal of stabilizing the private market through market segmentation.

title: Zoning Report: Massachusetts
affiliations: Land Use Atlas, Inc., Suffolk University Law School, Land Use Atlas, Inc., Independent and

detail.title: Zoning Report: Massachusetts

publicationDetails.detailsText: GWU Legal Studies Research Paper (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: George Washington University Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Massachusetts is facing a housing affordability crisis. Rising home prices and rents from Cape Cod to the Berkshires are pushing long-time residents out of their communities and harming local economies. While many factors inflate housing costs, locally adopted zoning rules regulating land uses, lots, and structures are one major contributor that is entirely within our control to change. Zoning codes are enforced in nearly every community across Massachusetts. And when they are used to ban apartments and small lot developments, they hike up costs by leaving residents with few options other than the most expensive type of housing: large-lot single-family homes. 

The Massachusetts state legislature has recognized the power of zoning to shape housing affordability. In 2021, legislators passed a zoning reform measure, the Massachusetts Bay Transit Authority (MBTA) Communities Act, which requires 177 jurisdictions in eastern Massachusetts to allow apartments near transit stations. At the time of the bill, they had only a partial picture of what zoning looked like across the state. Now, five years later, a first-of-its-kind dataset built by the National Zoning Atlas (NZA) allows us to take a step back and assess the state’s zoning landscape in full, measure the changes delivered by the MBTA Communities Act so far, and target future reform.

This report presents the first comprehensive, statewide analysis of zoning in Massachusetts. Building from our previous regional analysis, Zoning Report: Cape Cod, and drawing from the NZA database’s unprecedented ability to compare zoning codes across places through time, it identifies five key facts about how Massachusetts zones. 

Part I begins this report by exploring the state’s housing challenges and providing an overview of zoning’s influence on them.

Part II describes the NZA’s methodology for analyzing, digitizing, and updating zoning codes, highlighting land use issues unique to Massachusetts. This methodology enables data collection at an unprecedented scale, increasing public understanding of zoning through accessible visualizations and evidence-based analysis.

Part III details five key features about zoning conditions across Massachusetts today. It discusses the prevalence of zoning across the state, the strict limitations on where apartments can be built, the large minimum lot size requirements, the restrictions still placed on ADU construction despite the Affordable Homes Act, onerous parking requirements, and unit densities across Massachusetts’s Gateway Cities. Collectively, these rules severely constrain where diverse housing types can go.

Part IV turns to our assessment of the MBTA Communities Act. Taking advantage of our unique ability to compare zoning rules through time at scale, it discusses how zoning conditions have changed in the 115 MBTA communities that (a) adopted new zoning rules to come into full compliance with the law by December 2025 and (b) made their updated zoning text and map available to the public by that date. This Part reveals how this law has changed the region’s zoning landscape five years after it was adopted — and where it has fallen short.

Part V concludes the report with a set of actionable recommendations to support reforms to Massachusetts’s zoning framework, promote more accessible and affordable housing, and build communities that better reflect the needs and preferences of today’s residents.

title: Green Investment, Inequality and Misallocation
affiliations: Banque de France, Paris School of Economics (PSE)

detail.title: Green Investment, Inequality and Misallocation
detail.abstract: I propose a simple framework that accounts for many poverty-related empirical results in the literature on green investment and explains why ensuring a level playing field between the poor and the rich improves the economic and environmental efficiency of green investments. I depart from the traditional margin-based approach and focus on frictions. The poor have higher present biases and face higher interest rates, but under simplifying assumptions, the latter alone are important when deciding whether to invest in a green durable good. Non-discriminating subsidies favor the rich, who are more likely to choose green durable goods, but they incentivize the poor more strongly. Only full subsidies (i.e., subsidies that fully compensate for the initial price difference between green and brown durable goods) can ensure full allocative efficiency and fairness. Such full subsidies induce the systematic choice of the green durable good and are therefore not compatible with a positive private, social or environmental discount rate. The latter is defined as a social discount rate consistent with the net-zero target: it is lower than usual social discount rates, but is still positive in the presence of carbon capture technologies. Credit policies can ensure the allocative efficiency and fairness of a decentralized equilibrium over a wider range of situations.

title: P vs NP Problem in Portfolio Optimization: Integrating the Markowitz-CAPM Framework with Cardinality Constraints and Black-Scholes Derivative Pricing
