detail.abstract: This study develops an integrated economic-computational framework for portfolio construction that makes the P versus NP divide operational within a financially auditable Markowitz-CAPM setting. Starting from the convex mean-variance program, we impose a hard cardinality constraint |supp(w)| ≤ K, which couples discrete subset selection with continuous weight optimization and yields a mixed-integer quadratic program (MIQP). To ensure empirical transparency, the asset universe is built from approximately n≈94 U.S. industry portfolios from Aswath Damodaran, using levered betas and annualized equity volatilities to calibrate expected returns via μ_i = R_f + β_i•ERP and to construct a fully reconstructible covariance matrix through a single-index (market-model) structure. Because the resulting search space grows combinatorially (≈C(n,K)), the paper treats scalable optimization as an approximation problem and evaluates practical solution schemes-greedy screening, Monte Carlo sampling over K-subsets, and genetic algorithms-under a replication-oriented protocol with random-seed logging, distributional performance reporting (median/IQR/quantiles), convergence/effort curves, and runtime profiling. Dependence diagnostics (median pairwise correlation, tail correlation shares, eigenvalue concentration, PSD checks) are reported as first-class outputs to connect algorithmic behavior to the geometry implied by Σ. To support financial realism beyond linear assets, the framework is extended to a derivative-augmented universe by embedding a Black-Scholes European call as an additional instrument, mapped into CAPM-consistent moments via delta-based linearization and validated by moneyness-maturity robustness and a bump test (delta vs. repricing). Results demonstrate that (i) the hard cardinality rule materially reshapes attainable efficient frontiers and induces discontinuities relative to the unconstrained benchmark; (ii) heuristic performance must be assessed by stability and compute-cost trade-offs rather than single best-run outcomes; and (iii) under a single-index covariance, strong common-factor dependence limits diversification, explaining why high-β industries and clustered sectors may co-appear in K-sparse solutions. Overall, the paper provides a journal-grade, reproducible template for studying NP-hard portfolio selection with transparent inputs and extensible derivative overlays.

title: Objective vs. Perceived Corporate Greenness: Do Individuals Understand Corporate Sustainability Information?
affiliations: University of Bern and

detail.title: Objective vs. Perceived Corporate Greenness: Do Individuals Understand Corporate Sustainability Information?
detail.abstract: We investigate whether individuals correctly interpret corporate sustainability disclosures using a pre-registered survey experiment. We provide novel evidence that individuals can meaningfully differentiate emissions of firms along a greenness scale, even though their assessments exhibit a central tendency bias. This leads to overestimation of greenness among browner firms and underestimation among greener firms, with the bias disproportionately stronger for greener firms. We observe this bias even among finance professionals and sustainability experts. As a result, firms' financial incentives to invest in emissions reductions may be attenuated. However, we also demonstrate that some disclosure design features improve individuals' differentiation ability.

title: Issuer-Side Governance and IPO Price Formation: Evidence from Independent Advisers
affiliations: University of Oxford, Saïd Business School, University of Oxford - Said Business School and University of Oxford, Saïd Business School

detail.title: Issuer-Side Governance and IPO Price Formation: Evidence from Independent Advisers
detail.abstract: Issuer-side governance plays a central but understudied role in price formation in initial public offerings (IPOs). While the IPO literature primarily focuses on investor information production and underwriter incentives, issuers increasingly introduce an additional intermediary into the process: independent IPO advisers who oversee underwriter selection, investor engagement and pricing strategy. Using a new dataset on adviser participation in U.S. and European IPOs from 2010–2023 constructed from hand-collected advisory mandates and underwriting fee data, we document systematic differences between advised and non-advised offerings. Because adviser adoption is endogenous, however, such cross-sectional patterns may reflect underlying differences across offerings rather than the effects of advisory governance itself. Our empirical strategy leverages an institutional feature of IPO markets. Practitioner surveys and advisory fee structures suggest that advisory mandates become more prevalent once offerings reach a scale of roughly $250M, consistent with the fixed-cost nature of advisory services. In the data, adviser participation rises sharply around this deal-size scale. Using a fuzzy regression-kink design centered on this threshold, we examine how localized variation in adviser adoption around $250M relates to differences in IPO outcomes. Diagnostic tests show no evidence of manipulation or discontinuities in deal characteristics around the threshold. Applying this framework, two consistent patterns emerge. First, a one standard deviation increase in predicted adviser involvement is associated with a 4.80 percentage-point reduction in offer-price adjustments relative to the filing-range midpoint. Second, the same increase corresponds to approximately $19.1 million less underpricing for the average-sized IPO in our sample ($341 million), or a 5.61 percentage-point reduction in first-day returns. We find no corresponding association with underwriting spreads or withdrawal rates. These findings suggest that advisory governance is associated with earlier incorporation of information in the IPO process, and with reduced incentives for underwriters to underprice and strategically allocate shares. More broadly, the evidence highlights how issuer-side governance structures can influence both information aggregation and price formation in primary equity markets. These findings underscore the role of market design in shaping IPO price discovery.

title: Access Gained, Outcomes Unchanged: The Effects of ACA Medicaid Expansion on Self-Reported Mental Health

detail.title: Access Gained, Outcomes Unchanged: The Effects of ACA Medicaid Expansion on Self-Reported Mental Health

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether ACA Medicaid expansion improved self-reported mental health among low income non-elderly adults. Using BRFSS data from 2011 to 2019 and a difference-in-differences framework robust to staggered treatment timing, I estimate the effects of expansion on poor mental health days and frequent mental distress. Medicaid expansion increased insurance coverage by about 4 percentage points, reduced cost-related barriers to care by roughly 2 percentage points, and modestly increased routine checkups. Despite these improvements in access, I do not detect measurable improvements in broad self-reported mental health. The null results are stable across alternative control groups, event study specifications, robustness checks, and subgroup analyses. These findings suggest that expanding insurance improved financial access to care but was not, on its own, enough to generate measurable short-run gains in mental health. More broadly, the results are consistent with a setting in which provider capacity, treatment uptake, and other nonfinancial barriers limit the translation of coverage gains into better mental health outcomes.

title: Causal Machine Learning Reveals Divergent Effectiveness of Governance Modes for Sustainable Agricultural Transformation
affiliations: , McGill University - Department of Agricultural Economics, McGill University, Desautels Faculty of Management, Students and Independent

detail.title: Causal Machine Learning Reveals Divergent Effectiveness of Governance Modes for Sustainable Agricultural Transformation
detail.abstract: Agrifood structural transformation underpins progress toward Sustainable Development Goals, Yet whether the state should withdraw, deregulate, or inject this transition remains contested. We evaluate three governance modes across over 2,700 Chinese counties and two decades, applying Causal Forest with double/debiased machine learning to three policy reforms the 2006 agricultural tax abolition (withdraw), the 2016 supply-side reform (deregulate), and the 2014 targeted poverty alleviation campaign (inject). Governance design, not fiscal magnitude, determines effectiveness, and each mode’s impact is conditional on local institutional context: withdrawal accelerates the shift out of agriculture, where pre-reform distortions bind most tightly; deregulation diversifies cropping structures; yet injection produces no significant average effect, masking offsetting heterogeneity along fiscal-capacity lines. Data-driven targeting robustly outperforms administrative allocation in out-of-sample validation while disproportionately retaining the poorest counties. Sustainable agricultural transitions thus depend on the political economy of policy execution, not on spending magnitude.

detail.abstract: The effects of cities' expansion on sustainability, housing affordability, and carbon emissions are critical for formulating effective policies. This study examines the relationships between urban expansion and key outcomes such as CO₂ emissions, green space, and housing price-to-income ratios in cities in Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana. Standardized data on multiple urban indicators were analysed using linear regression, mediation analysis, and structural equation modelling (SEM) to separate direct and indirect effects. Regression results indicate that urban expansion increases CO₂ emissions and affects housing affordability, while built-up area and economic factors moderate these effects. Mediation analysis shows that infrastructure spending partially explains the effect of urban expansion on green space, though its impact on CO₂ emissions and housing affordability is limited. SEM confirms these findings, demonstrating strong explanatory power for CO₂ emissions and housing affordability and revealing interconnections between environmental and social outcomes. The study shows that rapid urban expansion can intensify environmental degradation and housing challenges, but targeted infrastructure investment can help mitigate these risks. These results provide empirical evidence to guide urban planning policies aimed at balancing growth, environmental sustainability, and housing affordability.

title: Rethinking Tobacco Control: The Global Case for Differentiated Regulation of Smoke-Free Alternatives
affiliations: Tel-Hai College and

detail.title: Rethinking Tobacco Control: The Global Case for Differentiated Regulation of Smoke-Free Alternatives

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Over the past years, governments have made substantial progress in tobacco control through higher taxes, advertising bans, and public smoking restrictions. Yet, in many advanced economies, smoking rates have stopped falling despite these strong measures. This stagnation suggests that traditional approaches, focused solely on discouraging all nicotine use, may have reached their limits. Simultaneously, the emergence of novel nicotine delivery systems-such as e-cigarettes, heated tobacco products, and nicotine pouches-has introduced a new dynamic. Although these products are not risk-free, they are generally associated with a significant reduction in toxicant exposure relative to conventional cigarettes. Policy responses to this technological development vary: some countries have adopted regulatory frameworks that differentiate products based on their relative health risks, while others apply uniform restrictions across all nicotine-containing products. This study analyzes the effect of these divergent regulatory frameworks on smoking prevalence across a cohort of 42 highly developed countries (Human Development Index (HDI) > 0.83). Using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression models controlling for development levels (measured by HDI index) and taxation levels, the findings indicate that countries adopting a differentiated, risk-proportionate policy exhibit smoking rates approximately 7 percentage points lower than those maintaining non-differentiated regulatory regimes. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that in this high-HDI cohort, differences in taxation levels alone no longer explain the variance in smoking prevalence, highlighting the importance of product substitution toward lower-risk nicotine products in sustaining progress in tobacco control.

title: The Elephant vs Donkey and Rank-and-file Employee Compensation
affiliations: California State University, San Marcos - College of Business Administration and San Diego State University

detail.title: The Elephant vs Donkey and Rank-and-file Employee Compensation
detail.abstract: We examine how executive political ideology shapes rank-and-file employee compensation. Using over 300,000 H-1B applications from 2010-2020, we document that firms led by Republican-leaning executives pay approximately 8% lower wages to H-1B workers than Democratic-leaning firms, after considering firm, job, and location characteristics. These findings align with agency theory and upper-echelons theory, which predict that managerial preferences influence organizational policies when discretion is high. Wage gaps intensify among financially constrained firms, firms with greater bargaining power, and in political environments with reduced scrutiny of rentextracting practices. The mechanism reflects managerial rent-seeking that leverages labor market frictions faced by H-1B workers. These compensation decisions carry real consequences: underpaying firms subsequently exhibit reduced innovation, lower valuations, and higher risks. Our findings show that executive political ideology has a significant influence on rank-and-file employee compensation, which affects worker productivity and firm performance.

title: From Musk's Prophecy to Human Nature Institutionalism: A New Governance Paradigm for "Technology-Society" Imbalance in the AI Era

detail.title: From Musk's Prophecy to Human Nature Institutionalism: A New Governance Paradigm for "Technology-Society" Imbalance in the AI Era
detail.abstract: Focusing on the "technology-society" imbalance risk revealed by Elon Musk's AGI prophecy, this paper analyzes the impact of the capital-technology binding model on labor-capital balance, wealth distribution and institutional systems, proposes and systematically expounds the governance scheme of Human Nature Institutionalism with "short-sighted human nature" as the axiomatic starting point and "three theorems and two lemmas" as the core framework, and demonstrates the necessity and feasibility of this new governance paradigm centered on "human nature adaptation" for avoiding the risks of technological monopoly and social rift and guiding the society towards a "people-oriented" development direction. The research shows that the deep-seated crisis in the AI era stems from the double mismatch between the traditional governance paradigm and the laws of human behavior as well as the speed of technological change. By integrating multidisciplinary resources such as behavioral science, Marxist human studies, traditional Chinese people-oriented thought, philosophical anthropology and evolutionary psychology, Human Nature Institutionalism systematically injects the laws of human nature into institutional design, and constructs a four-dimensional governance system of "human nature adaptationtechnology guidance-fairness guarantee-rationality cultivation", providing an original theoretical tool and practical path for solving the predicament of the prophecy that "great wealth coexists with social rift".

detail.abstract: We study the long-run health effects of illegal toxic waste disposal conducted by organized crime in Italy. We exploit quasi-random variation in historical wind direction around contaminated sites combined with a difference-in-differences design. Using administrative cancer mortality data spanning four decades, we find that wind exposure to pollutants stemming from the contaminated sites increases cancer mortality substantially. The effects emerge after long latencies and grow over time. In later years, wind exposure implies roughly two additional cancer deaths per municipality-year relative to unexposed municipalities equally proximate to contaminated sites. Our findings reveal a previously unmeasured health externality of organized crime.

detail.abstract: Agri-environmental programs aimed at working farmland have played an increasingly significant role in agricultural support policies within developed countries. A critical issue that arises correspondingly is the efficiency of these programs in allocating spending, particularly regarding the additionality of agri-environmental subsidies. This paper focuses on the Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program (CREP) in Maryland, specifically subsidies for the installation of riparian buffers. We provide estimates of additionality using: (i) a first-difference estimator applied to panel data and (ii) semiparametric and parametric estimators applied to cross-sectional data. All results indicate that CREP offers modest additionality, with estimates ranging from 65% to 70% that are robust across a variety of model specifications.

title: Breaking the Deadlock with Human Nature Institutionalism: From "Buried" to "Empowered" Original Talents

detail.title: Breaking the Deadlock with Human Nature Institutionalism: From "Buried" to "Empowered" Original Talents
detail.abstract: Aiming at the "Ye Gong's love for dragons" dilemma in the current scientific research field, where the slogan of "supporting originality" is disconnected from practice, this paper takes human nature institutionalism as an analytical tool to decode the root causes of three major splits in the scientific research ecosystem: the split between value advocacy and assessment logic, the split between the demand for talent spotters and the risk of identifying talents, and the split between academic laws and administrative control. It points out that the core crux lies in the deviation of institutional design from the underlying axiom of "human nature being myopic, pursuing immediate interests and avoiding harms". Based on the three theorems, two lemmas and the "melon-slicing theory" of human nature institutionalism, this paper proposes the "China Annual Original Talent Selection Competition" mechanism. By reconstructing the incentives for talent spotters, empowering original talents and optimizing the efficiency of research funds, this mechanism realizes the adaptation between institutions and human nature. This mechanism is not a castle in the air, but an upgrading of existing talent selection practices. It also faces potential challenges such as review impartiality and fund control, and ensures sustainability through a dynamic constraint mechanism. The research provides theoretical support and practical paths for solving the dilemma of buried original talents and improving the efficiency of research funds.

title: No. 1 in the Series of Human Nature Institutionalism: StudiesCross-Racial Myopia Coefficient (δ) Calibration Method and Empirical Verification

detail.title: No. 1 in the Series of Human Nature Institutionalism: StudiesCross-Racial Myopia Coefficient (δ) Calibration Method and Empirical Verification
detail.abstract: Shortsighted pursuit of gain and avoidance of harm" is a common trait of all humanity. As a key indicator quantifying human nature, the myopia coefficient (δ) holds core guiding significance in cross-racial institutional design. However, current measurements of δ coefficients across different races/regions lack a unified standard, and existing studies have not established a calibration framework that balances "common human nature + subtle racial differences". This research constructs a minimalist calibration model of "global benchmark value + racial correction coefficient", adopts a "neuro-behavioral-historical" three-dimensional triangulation model to measure the racial correction coefficient (k), and verifies the model's effectiveness through both conventional cross-racial institutional cases and quasi-natural experiments (DID). The study determines the global myopia coefficient benchmark value δ_base = 0.2, with racial correction coefficients of 0.95, 1.02, and 1.01 for Asian, European, and African races respectively. The calibration results are proven robust through stability tests. This method provides a unified "measurement standard" for the cross-scenario application of human nature institutionalism, and can be widely used in traditional public policy, digital governance, AI institutional optimization and other emerging fields.

title: Constructing a Human Nature Adaptability Review Mechanism Based on Human Nature Institutionalism: A Rigorous Path to Implement the "People-Centered" Philosophy

detail.title: Constructing a Human Nature Adaptability Review Mechanism Based on Human Nature Institutionalism: A Rigorous Path to Implement the "People-Centered" Philosophy
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a native Chinese original institutional economics theory—Human Nature Institutionalism, which for the first time identifies "human myopia and the tendency to seek advantage and avoid harm" as the core axiom of institutional economics. It constructs a complete logical system of "axiom-theorem-lemma-tool", breaking through the limitations of previous institutional economics and behavioral economics that focused on multi-phenomenal analysis of human nature. This axiom is empirically verified through multiple disciplines including evolutionary biology, neuroscience, and behavioral economics, based on which an operable "Human Nature Adaptability (θ) Review Mechanism" is derived. The core innovation of this paper lies in achieving three major transcendences: the positional upgrade from individual preferences to group axioms, the theoretical upgrade from descriptive theories to deductive systems, and the application upgrade from single tools to comprehensive solutions. Compared with the hyperbolic discounting theory in behavioral economics, Human Nature Institutionalism not only accurately refines the fundamental logic of group human nature but also provides a comprehensive institutional solution applicable to multiple scenarios such as public policy, organizational incentives, and social governance. By designing a lightweight "policy laboratory" launch method and a phased implementation roadmap, combined with dynamic optimization of the θ indicator through a digital governance platform, this mechanism can fundamentally adjust the incentive structure, resolve involution, and promote the unification of individual and collective interests, providing a Chinese institutional economics solution for advancing the modernization of the national governance system and governance capacity. This paper clarifies the theoretical boundaries between Human Nature Institutionalism and traditional institutional economics, as well as its applicable scenarios and limitations, achieving an organic combination of theoretical innovation and practical application.

detail.title: The Competition Laws and Intellectual Property Rights in Bangladesh: Aligning Innovation with Fair Markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: (2024 – 2025) 10 City University of Hong Kong Law Review 75–100.

detail.abstract: The intellectual property regime of Bangladesh has gone through significant amendments in 2023 since a series of Acts were passed by the parliament to strengthen its commitment to protect and promote innovation. Though competition law got its formal recognition in 2012, it has secured considerable attention in legal discourse as a tool to create fair market practices. This article strives to find out potential disputes between the move to protect intellectual property rights ("IPRs") and the restrictive measures under competition laws. It further explores the challenges to deal with this issue including the jurisdictional differences, troubled enforcement mechanisms, limitations as to extents and scopes of applying antitrust laws by the courts. Against this backdrop, the article offers a set of rational reforms aimed to harmonize competition laws with IPRs. The reforms include revising existing legislation[s] strengthening adjudicatory mechanisms and promoting institutional coordination. By addressing the tensions and proposing reasonable reforms, this article aims to facilitate the evolution of a more impactful IP and competition regime in Bangladesh.

title: Cartel Management Services
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

detail.title: Cartel Management Services
detail.abstract: Cartel management services are intermediaries that coordinate competitors’ pricing through centralized software. Our comparative analysis of US and EU law argues that algorithmic cartel management falls squarely within established and commonly held antitrust principles. Existing U.S. and E.U. antitrust doctrine already condemns such arrangements when they substitute coordinated implementation for independent decision-making.  The most serious issue is determining when a practice moves from non-coercive exchange of information to actual coordination. The Article develops a functional framework distinguishing lawful information provision from unlawful cartel administration, centered on whether intermediaries operationalize coordination through delegation, defaults, monitoring, or compliance inducements.

title: The Essence and Reality of Belief from the Perspective of Human Nature Institutionalism

detail.title: The Essence and Reality of Belief from the Perspective of Human Nature Institutionalism
detail.abstract: Belief is not a transcendent spiritual sublimity, but a dynamic choice resulting from the interaction between the core axiom of "myopic human nature pursuing immediate interests and avoiding harms," the duality of human nature (self-interest and altruism, sociality and individuality), institutional design, cultural values, and the real environment. Taking human nature institutionalism as the analytical framework, this paper integrates the three-dimensional interest perception function of "monetary income (I) + emotional value (E) + social recognition value (S)" to construct a complete system of "axiom-theorem-constraint-moderating variable-measurement tool." Through three core theorems (motivation attenuation, institutional swing, and institutional efficiency), it systematically explains the utilitarian essence and normal distribution characteristics of belief. The study finds that most people's beliefs follow the logic of "priority to immediate interests," and their interest perception is moderated by the myopia coefficient (δ): high-δ groups rely more on E and S, while low-δ groups focus more on I. The effectiveness of institutions depends on the comprehensive adaptation to three-dimensional interests and the balance of human nature's duality; excessive constraint or laissez-faire will lead to belief alienation. Digital technology not only provides a new path of "immediate feedback" for belief guidance but also harbors the risk of institutional alienation. This paper refutes cognitive misunderstandings such as "Chinese people have no beliefs" and "belief = money worship," and proposes a three-dimensional guidance path of "multi-dimensional interest adaptation + dual balance of human nature + risk avoidance." It emphasizes that institutional design should attach equal importance to "adapting to human nature" and "guiding goodness,"providing theoretical support and operable schemes for the modernization of national governance and cross-cultural belief harmony.

title: The Grammar of Order: The Adhesive Principle in Complex Systems
affiliations: and Soochow University

detail.title: The Grammar of Order: The Adhesive Principle in Complex Systems
detail.abstract: Zipf's Law reveals the universal distribution of "the frequent few" but stops at phenomenological description; complex systems theory explores systemic emergence yet often overlooks the simplicity of its core architecture. The "Adhesive Theory" proposed in this paper aims to bridge this logical gap: any stably existing complex system must contain a small number of "adhesive nodes" with "asymmetric hubness" and "low-cost connectivity." Their core function is to anchor the system structure and optimize factor aggregation at the lowest internal friction cost, with other elements in the system distributed orderly around these nodes. This theory breaks through the disciplinary limitations of Zipf's Law, discovering a unified "structural grammar" across physical forces, chemical bonds, and social institutions. It not only addresses doubts about the emergence and teleology of cross-level systems but also constructs a qualitative-quantitative analytical framework. Serving as a general analytical tool for explaining historical order changes, current platform governance dilemmas, and future social evolution, it proposes three theoretically counterintuitive predictions, upgrading the explanatory framework into an ideological engine driving future research.

title: Intellectual Property Financing, Innovation, and Aggregate TFP
affiliations: and City University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Intellectual Property Financing, Innovation, and Aggregate TFP
detail.abstract: We study how expanding access to intellectual property (IP)-backed credit affects firm innovation and aggregate total factor productivity (TFP). Exploiting China's IP-backed financing pilot as a quasi-natural experiment, we use difference-indifferences estimates to show that the policy increases R&D participation, raises firm-level productivity, and reduces capital misallocation. To interpret these effects and quantify their aggregate implications, we develop a dynamic model of heterogeneous firms that borrow subject to collateral constraints backed by tangible assets and IP, and choose R&D investment and the accumulation of wealth. R&D raises future productivity and creates collateralizable IP. We estimate the model by the method of simulated moments, using the policy-induced shift in R&D participation to identify the change in IP pledgeability. The estimated model implies that a nationwide adoption of IP-backed financing would raise long-run TFP by 14%, with roughly two-thirds coming from static gains due to improved capital allocation and the remainder from dynamic gains driven by higher innovation that accumulate over time. Relative to a comparable expansion of lending backed by tangible collateral, IP-backed financing delivers larger productivity gains by easing constraints for high-productivity but low-wealth firms and by strengthening incentives to accumulate IP as collateral for future borrowing.

title: No. 3 in the Series of Human Nature Institutionalism Studies: Construction of a Quantitative Model for Environmental Uncertainty(ξ):Dynamic Measurement Based on Conflict, Inflation, and Social Media, and Its Application in Human Nature Institutionalism

detail.title: No. 3 in the Series of Human Nature Institutionalism Studies: Construction of a Quantitative Model for Environmental Uncertainty(ξ):Dynamic Measurement Based on Conflict, Inflation, and Social Media, and Its Application in Human Nature Institutionalism

keywords.keywords: Environmental Uncertainty; Human Nature Institutionalism; Short-sighted Coefficient; Polynomial Chaos Expansion; Sobol Sensitivity Index; Institutional Dynamics; Multilingual Sentiment Analysis; Computable Institutional Science; Regionally Differentiated Governance; Long-cycle Robustness

detail.abstract: This study stems from a core theoretical dilemma in "Human Nature Institutionalism": as a key variable, environmental uncertainty (ξ) has long remained an abstract concept, hindering the empirical testing and application of the theory. The research aims to construct a dynamically updatable ξ quantitative model that balances global commonalities with regional differences and covers long-cycle characteristics. Drawing on complex scientific methods, the model integrates three dimensions—global conflict index (structural disturbance), core inflation rate (cyclical fluctuation), and social media sentiment (perceptual amplification)—adopts Polynomial Chaos Expansion (PCE) to handle their nonlinear interactions, and introduces a dynamic weight adjustment mechanism based on Sobol sensitivity index (ξ ∈ [0,2], quantifying the degree to which the environment reinforces short-sighted human nature). By integrating empirical findings from neuroeconomics, evolutionary psychology, and behavioral economics across disciplines, the global benchmark short-sighted coefficient δ_base = 0.2 (95% confidence interval [0.192, 0.208]) is systematically calibrated, providing a scientific benchmark for the attenuation coefficient α = δ×ξ. Through retrospective testing of global data from 2000 to 2023, local calculation case verification in high-conflict regions of the Middle East, and offline simulation of major historical events in the 20th century (World War II, collapse of the Bretton Woods system), combined with robustness tests across six dimensions, the validity and stability of the model are fully confirmed. Results show that the ξ_PCE index explains 0.68-0.78 of institutional effectiveness, significantly outperforming traditional uncertainty indices (EPU, VIX); α = δ×ξ has a significant linear and nonlinear positive impact on policy attenuation rate, and immediate feedback-based policies can mitigate 37.5%-44.7% of the attenuation effect. Technically, an innovative multilingual contextual drift processing strategy is adopted, increasing the recognition accuracy of non-English texts to ≥0.80, while establishing sound data ethics norms. This study not only provides key quantitative infrastructure for "Human Nature Institutionalism" and opens up a new path for "Computable Institutional Science" but also refines an "ξ index-driven institutional design optimization process," offering actionable quantitative tools for global governance, regional policy-making, and historical experience learning. It demonstrates the original contribution of China's independent knowledge system in the field of social sciences.

title: No. 2 in the Series of Human Nature Institutionalism Studies: On the Constituent Dimensions of the "Interest Perception Function V": Measuring Immediate Emotional and Social Identity Values Beyond Monetary Returns Based on the Axiom of Myopic Human Nature

detail.title: No. 2 in the Series of Human Nature Institutionalism Studies: On the Constituent Dimensions of the "Interest Perception Function V": Measuring Immediate Emotional and Social Identity Values Beyond Monetary Returns Based on the Axiom of Myopic Human Nature

keywords.keywords: Interest Perception Function; Human Nature Institutionalism; Axiom of Myopic Human Nature; Emotional Value; Social Identity; Non-Monetary Return Measurement; Institutional Fit; Myopia Coefficient; Dimension Weight; Interdisciplinary Integration

detail.abstract: Based on the "axiom of myopic human nature" in human nature institutionalism, traditional interest perception functions are confined to the dimension of monetized returns and thus struggle to explain non-monetarily driven decision-making phenomena. This paper proposes a "three-dimensional integrated" interest perception function model: V=w1×I+w2×E+w3×S, deconstructing interest perception into three core dimensions: monetary returns (I), emotional value (E), and social identity value (S). Here, w1, w2, and w3 are relative weights moderated by the myopia coefficient (δ), and there is no mandatory normalization to retain situational flexibility. A theoretical framework is constructed through a critical literature review integrating interdisciplinary achievements, and empirical testing is conducted using a mixed-method approach of "behavioral experiments + physiological measurements + questionnaires," combined with publicly available authoritative data and original experimental data from 500 participants. The results show that: (1) All three dimensions independently and positively drive the total perceived value (V), with the weight order in the baseline scenario being w2 (0.42) > w1 (0.38) > w3 (0.31); (2) The myopia coefficient (δ) has a significant moderating effect—high-δ groups are more dependent on emotional and social identity values (w2+w3≈0.84), while low-δ groups focus more on monetary returns (w1≈0.47); (3) There are substitution/complementarity effects among the three dimensions: non-monetary dimensions can effectively substitute for monetary returns in high-δ groups, and multi-dimensional combinations exhibit a synergistic amplification effect in low-δ groups. The revised function breaks through the limitation of "monetary supremacy" and can be directly incorporated into the core theorems of institutional dynamics, providing a micro-foundation for quantifying the degree of institutional-human nature fit (θ). By operationalizing "interest" as a measurable multi-dimensional construct, this study aims to lay a solid micro-foundation for the quantitative evaluation of "institutional-human nature fit" and promote institutional design from experience-based to science-based. This research not only provides a more scientific measurement tool for "interest" but also raises fundamental questions about the traditional policy evaluation paradigm based on the "rational man" assumption, laying the cornerstone for constructing a "human nature-centered" institutional science.

title: Criminalizing Failure to Yield to Pedestrians at Zebra Crossings: Fortifying the Life Defense Line for Pedestrians with the Governance Logic of Drunk Driving Criminalization

detail.title: Criminalizing Failure to Yield to Pedestrians at Zebra Crossings: Fortifying the Life Defense Line for Pedestrians with the Governance Logic of Drunk Driving Criminalization
detail.abstract: To address the high incidence of casualties caused by motor vehicles failing to yield to pedestrians at zebra crossings, this paper adopts the methods of statistical data analysis, jurisprudential discrimination and practical research, sorts out the public data released by national and local traffic management departments since 2020, compares the regulatory differences between drunk driving and failure to yield at zebra crossings, and clarifies the risk attribute of intentional failure to yield at zebra crossings in specific scenarios. Based on the governance practices in various regions, a detailed institutional design for criminalization is proposed, and core questions such as law enforcement costs and the balance of road rights between pedestrians and motor vehicles are responded to. The research shows that the number of casualties caused by failure to yield at zebra crossings has long been higher than that by drunk driving, and the current result-oriented liability model lacks effective deterrence. Intentional failure to yield when pedestrians have entered the zebra crossing poses an immediate and definite high risk, which warrants the same criminal regulation as drunk driving. The precise criminalization scheme proposed in this paper can provide practical reference for the improvement of road traffic rule of law and safety governance.

title: The First Algorithmic Standard of Systemic Resilience for Global Settlements and Sustainable Debt Resolution

detail.title: The First Algorithmic Standard of Systemic Resilience for Global Settlements and Sustainable Debt Resolution
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of SV-1.0 Stablecoin-the world's first settlement unit whose value is determined not by trust in a single issuer or speculative demand, but by objective, verifiable systemic resilience of a global basket of 195 countries. Unlike traditional stablecoins (USDT, USDC), cryptocurrencies (Bitcoin), and national currencies (USD, EUR), SV-1.0 Stablecoin combines algorithmic stability based on verifiable data, an early-warning mechanism for crises (94% accuracy, 11-month lead time), built-in regulatory compliance via the LC multiplier (Basel IV, FATF, ESG), global diversification without loss of national sovereignty, and an integrated mechanism for sustainable global debt resolution. Based on retrospective analysis of 100 historical crises (1970-2024), the methodology demonstrates 94% prediction accuracy with an average lead time of 11 months. Technical infrastructure is fully ready for deployment: smart contracts, oracle network, stabilization mechanisms, and regulatory documentation are in the final preparation stage. This edition includes comprehensive analysis of how SV-1.0 addresses the global debt crisis ($315 trillion outstanding), identifies potential opposition forces, explains why cooperation benefits all stakeholders, and quantifies creditor gains from participation. The paper also provides comparative analysis of exchange rate dynamics relative to 50+ fiat currencies, 10 crypto assets, and existing stablecoins, as well as stress-testing results under extreme scenarios. Conclusion: SV-1.0 Stablecoin represents not a competing asset, but an infrastructural standard that can be integrated into existing financial systems to enhance transparency, resilience, and efficiency of international settlements and sustainable debt resolution.

title: The Intergenerational Transmission of Health in the Long-Run: Exploring Dynamic Patterns Across Africa

detail.title: The Intergenerational Transmission of Health in the Long-Run: Exploring Dynamic Patterns Across Africa
detail.abstract: Africa remains the poorest and one of the most unequal regions globally, with limited upward mobility and strong intergenerational persistence of disadvantage. Child health is a key channel of transmission, shaping later outcomes in education, labour force participation, and earnings. This paper investigates long-run trends in the intergenerational transmission of health across 29 African countries over 1975-2015, using 123 rounds of the Demographic and Health Surveys covering more than three million children. I measure child health by under-five mortality and maternal health by adult height. Results show strong persistence: taller mothers have significantly lower child mortality, with effects varying across countries and correlated with development levels. Over time, persistence first increased, then declined from the mid-1990s, consistent with the inverse care law. A dynamic panel analysis reveals that healthcare provision, education, institutional quality, and inequality-rather than GDP alone-explain these heterogeneous trajectories. Convergence tests suggest conditional convergence, with countries clustering into distinct mobility clubs. The findings underscore the role of structural and institutional factors in shaping intergenerational health mobility.

title: Institutional Learning and Volatility Transmission in ASEAN Equity Markets: A Network-Integrated Regime-Dependent Approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Institutional Learning and Volatility Transmission in ASEAN Equity Markets: A Network-Integrated Regime-Dependent Approach
detail.abstract: Most existing studies on emerging-market volatility treat institutional quality as a lowfrequency, static background variable, leaving them unable to characterize how institutions adjust in real time to crises, policy signals, and information shocks, or how such adjustments shape cross-market volatility transmission. This paper constructs a MIDAS-based highfrequency institutional learning index derived from economic policy uncertainty (EPU) and introduces two new volatility modeling frameworks: the Institutional Response Dynamics Model (IRDM), which captures the short-run institutional reaction mechanism, and the Network-Integrated IRDM (N-IRDM), which describes the synchronous propagation of institutional responses across markets. Using daily data for Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand from 2010-2024, our empirical results show that institutional learning amplifies the immediate volatility response to shocks but subsequently accelerates volatility normalization; that crisis-memory terms exhibit strong persistence; and that network mechanisms significantly improve tail-fit accuracy and short-term forecasting, especially during multi-country crisis episodes. Placebo-network and lagged-network tests further reveal that cross-market institutional spillovers primarily reflect regional common-factor synchronicity rather than dependence on any specific correlation structure. Based on this evidence, we conclude that (i) enhancing transparency and policy-guidance consistency can mitigate the short-run amplification induced by institutional learning, (ii) improving crisis-related information disclosure can weaken the prolonged volatility associated with crisis memory, (iii) strengthening regional regulatory coordination can dampen the synchronous amplification of institutional reactions, and (iv) systematic monitoring of institution-and information-based common factors can help identify early stages of region-wide risk escalation.

title: Human Capital Capacity Restructuring in the AI Era: Mechanisms and Paths of Educational Transformation and Demographic Dividend Conversion

detail.title: Human Capital Capacity Restructuring in the AI Era: Mechanisms and Paths of Educational Transformation and Demographic Dividend Conversion
detail.abstract: Against the dual backdrop of building a powerful education country and the in-depth transformation of the AI industry, a striking contradiction has emerged in China between the employment predicament of over ten million college graduates and the talent demand gap of enterprises. This contradiction is essentially a structural mismatch between the industrial-era education system and the human capital demand in the AI era, also highlighting the urgency of transforming the quantitative demographic dividend into a qualitative one. Based on the human capital theory, endogenous growth theory and the development laws of digital education, combined with authoritative data from the Ministry of Education, the National Bureau of Statistics and practical cases of universities, enterprises and local governments, this paper analyzes the capacity mismatch problem caused by the lag of educational transformation in the AI era, and points out that the core proposition of education reform in the last window period of the demographic dividend is to realize the transformation of human capital training mode from "knowledge indoctrination" to "capacity restructuring". The study proposes that we should take the reform of the education system as the core, build a collaborative human capital improvement system involving universities, enterprises, the government and society, and promote the accurate alignment between educational transformation and industrial demand through paths such as interdisciplinary training, industry-education integration training and inclusive policy guarantee, so as to realize the effective transformation of demographic dividend into talent dividend, and lay a solid human capital foundation for building a powerful education country and enhancing national competitiveness in the AI era.

title: Family Ownership, ESG Strategies, and Corporate Risk-Taking: Econometric and Machine Learning Evidence
affiliations: Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l., Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro, LUM Jean Monnet university, Niccolò Cusano University and University of Catania

detail.title: Family Ownership, ESG Strategies, and Corporate Risk-Taking: Econometric and Machine Learning Evidence
detail.abstract: The present study aims to contribute to the exploration of the combined effect of sustainability strategies and family governance on corporate risk-taking, with a focus on the temporal dimension of ESG engagement and the multidimensional nature of family involvement. Although a number of research papers have attempted to investigate the interrelations between ESG performance, corporate risk, and ownership structure, the existing research is fragmented, static, and limited in terms of its research methodology. Therefore, this article aims to provide a framework that (a) distinguishes between longterm and short-term ESG performance and (b) distinguishes between ownership incentives and management control in family firms. The present study uses a sample of listed corporations and combines three different research methods: fixed effects panel regressions, cluster analysis, and machine learning regression methods. The results of this study suggest that long-term ESG performance is negatively related to corporate risk, as proxied by the volatility of operating performance. The effect of short-term ESG performance on corporate risk is less robust and less consistent. Furthermore, this study finds that family cash-flow rights and family CEOs are negatively related to corporate risk, in accordance with the SEW hypothesis. Finally, this study reveals that the positive interaction effect of long-term ESG performance and family cash-flow rights mitigates the negative effect of sustainability on corporate risk in family-controlled corporations. The results of this study show that cluster analysis reveals a high degree of heterogeneity in corporate strategic profiles, with different clusters characterized by specific configurations of ESG orientation, family involvement, corporate governance structure, firm size, and corporate risk. The results of this study also show that the proposed model has a high predictive power in relation to corporate risk levels, as indicated by the results of the random forest regression analysis. Finally, this study reveals that financial fundamentals are more important in determining corporate risk than ESG engagement and family control; however, ESG engagement and family control are secondary but significant and nonlinear determinants of corporate risk.

title: Employee Engagement in the Home-Work Lifeworld: Graham Employee Engagement Scale
affiliations: University of Saskatchewan

detail.title: Employee Engagement in the Home-Work Lifeworld: Graham Employee Engagement Scale
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic caused a rapid implementation of the work-from-home model. The struggles imposed by COVID-19 and the challenges of the work-from-home pose consequences for being either fully present and complete or fragmented when occupying an organizational role. This article summarizes existing knowledge on employee engagement under the work-from-home design. In addition, it provides new insights and coherent explanations on the development of engagement when employees are working from home. This article offers a conceptual framework regarding employee engagement and the workfrom-home format, i.e., the homework lifeworld matrix. The homework lifeworld matrix describes and explains the processes or sequence of events while employees work from home. The homework lifeworld matrix provides a basis for understanding the underlying constructs of engagement; body, time, space, and relations and their interconnectedness when employees work from home. The article presents the definitions of employee engagement and the Graham Employee Engagement Scale for assessing and developing employee engagement. Specifically, this article proposes that engagement should be assessed holistically by considering different facets of the body, time, space, and relations and specifies the practical ways for managing employees in home-based work.

detail.abstract:
Strategic management is fundamentally defined as the art and science of formulating, implementing, and evaluating cross-functional decisions that empower an organization to achieve its long-term objectives (David & David, 2017). This discipline represents the comprehensive management of an organization’s overall long-term purpose, distinct from the daily management of routine operations (Witcher, 2020). In the contemporary global landscape, the subject is characterized by theoretical shifts and methodological wars, demanding that the management of operations today takes full account of the strategic management of tomorrow (Witcher, 2020). Tesla, Inc. serves as a primary example of how a purpose-driven organization can leverage strategic change defined as transformational repositioning designed to move an organization to a new and sustainable competitive position to dominate emerging industries (Witcher, 2020).

Tesla’s expansion into the People’s Republic of China, specifically highlighted by the inauguration of the Shanghai Energy Storage Megafactory in February 2025, underscores the critical importance of situational analysis. Strategic management requires an organization to evaluate its current external and internal situations to develop strategic objectives that guide the long-term journey (Witcher, 2020,). In 2024, Tesla achieved a record-breaking performance in China, selling over 657,000 vehicles, an 8.8% year-on-year increase, even as global deliveries experienced their first annual decline (The Straits Times, 2025; Moomoo, 2025). This performance highlights China as a cornerstone of Tesla’s global-level strategy, the strategic management of operations across multinational borders accounting for 36.7% of total global deliveries in 2024 and rising to 38.24% in 2025 (Witcher, 2020; The Straits Times, 2025; Tesery, 2026). The following analysis critically examines the mechanisms of this success through the lenses of strategic alliances, resource identification, and the rigorous evaluation of competitive advantage using established management frameworks.

The model is built on five foundational mechanisms: Neutral Mirror, Coherent Tourbillon, Stable Neutralion, Proportional EPA (Elasticity of Perceptual Alignment), and the Single Axis Principle, which together define the minimum conditions for non‑contractive structures. The Axial Continuity Codex is proposed as a conceptual standard for analyzing high‑field cognitive, institutional, and theoretical systems.

title: Stochastic Discount Factor Analysis in Commodity Asset Pricing
affiliations: , Brunel University London and Brunel University London

detail.title: Stochastic Discount Factor Analysis in Commodity Asset Pricing
detail.abstract: We develope the Stochastic Discount Factor (SDF) copula analysis as a diagnostic framework to visualize whether dependence between returns and the SDF is primarily driven by exposure or by pricing. The distinction between exposure and pricing follows from the linear factor structure and the SDF representation, while the copula-based analysis provides a complementary way to represent it. We consider standard return-based factor models commonly used to study market integration in commodity markets. We show that the sum of the factor realizations depends only on exposures and explains return variability regardless of whether factors are priced. By contrast, the dependence between the SDF and returns, measured through copula correlation, depends directly on which factors are priced in the model.

title: Climate Disasters and Intergenerational Equity: A Fiscal Rule for Sustainable Development
affiliations: Columbia University, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Department of Economics, National University Singapore and Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Climate Disasters and Intergenerational Equity: A Fiscal Rule for Sustainable Development
detail.abstract: Climate disasters threaten intergenerational equity by exposing future generations to rising risks. We develop a model in which a government learns about disaster risk and enforces a sustainability criterion requiring expected social welfare to be non-decreasing over time. This criterion-similar to the principle underlying the UN Sustainable Development Goals-can be decentralized through state-contingent fiscal instruments: when perceived disaster risk is high, the constraint binds and government raises a consumption tax to finance investment subsidies for resilience. Such a fiscal rule leads to intergenerational-welfare smoothing and improves asset valuations despite adverse climate news due to commitments to future resilience. Compared with a government that adopts a social discount rate lower than households', the sustainability-constraint rule responds more sensitively to disaster risk and is better aligned with observed consumption-based climate-resilience taxes, such as those implemented in Greece and Spain.

detail.abstract: Between 2020 and 2026, social media platforms have produced a new form of informal justice system driven by influencers, online activists, and digital audiences. These actors increasingly shape public opinion, reputations, and economic outcomes without institutional oversight. This dissertation investigates the emergence of digital vigilantism and the question of moral authority in influencer-led accountability movements. Using interdisciplinary perspectives from philosophy, sociology, media studies, psychology, and digital governance, the research examines how online call-out culture operates, how outrage spreads, and how reputational damage occurs in the absence of due process. Drawing on real global and Nigerian case studies-including the #JusticeForMohbad movement (Nigeria, 2023-2025), the Johnny Depp vs Amber Heard livestreamed trial (United States, 2022), high-profile "cancel culture" incidents, and social-media-accelerated financial panic events such as the Silicon Valley Bank bank run (United States, March 2023)-the dissertation argues that social media has created a parallel justice system without procedural safeguards. The dissertation concludes that while influencer activism can expose wrongdoing and strengthen consumer and civic pressure, weak accountability mechanisms, algorithmic incentives for outrage, and parasocial mobilisation risks transforming justice into spectacle and moral authority into performance.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we consider the evolution of UEFA competitions for the last 25 years. We find that because of the use of the “league coefficient” in granting direct access to clubs from the highest ranking leagues, access to the Champions league (CL) has had a strong self-reinforcing element so that participation in one year increases the likelihood of participation in subsequent years. We also find that the scope of direct access has been enlarged over time and that the distribution of prize money has become more unequal at least within the CL. These factors are likely to explain the increased entrenchment of participants that we observe in the CL. The emergence of a relatively narrow group of repeat participants in the CL also appears to contribute to the deterioration of competitive balance that we observe  in national competitions (in particular in the top 5 leagues, namely England, Spain, Germany, Italy and France) as the outcome of confrontations between these clubs and other participants in national leagues becomes highly predictable.  Overall, UEFA’s governance of European competition challenges the value and maintenance of competitive balance in national competitions.

detail.abstract: Roughly 25% of older Americans have diabetes. OLS estimates indicate that diabetes is associated with a roughly ten percentage point reduction in employment and this effect has been constant for decades. Estimating its causal effect is challenging because diabetes is correlated with health behaviors and early-life conditions that also shape labor market outcomes. Using thirty years of data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS), I implement an imperfect instrumental variables (IIV) approach to bound the causal effect of diabetes on employment. I study how these bounds evolve across the decades using smoking as an IIV. I justify this choice using a life-cycle model and a first stage statistical test. For men, smoking-based bounds are informative in all waves and consistently imply upper bounds much closer to zero than the corresponding OLS estimates, ruling out large negative causal effects and suggesting that selection plays an important role in explaining the core correlation.

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved a voluntary survey of youth participants across nine countries. All participants were informed of the research purpose, and data were collected anonymously to ensure privacy. No personally identifiable information was stored or shared, and participation was entirely optional.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. All data collection and analysis were conducted using the internal resources and volunteer network of the Youth Economics Initiative. Specifically, Mahesh Yandra created a survey with questions regarding the topic then was distributed through YEI's clubs and social media to collect responses. Responses were utilized to create the research paper.

detail.abstract: This report analyzes financial behaviors, literacy levels, and spending habits across youth respondents from 9+ countries. The data shows a clear link between savings behavior and self-reported financial confidence. In fact, 43% of respondents reported high confidence, especially if they stick to strict savings habits. However, this confidence doesn't necessarily translate to action. While 41% of students claim to understand investment basics, only 20% are utilizing their money to invest. This gap highlights a critical failure in current youth financial education systems to move students from knowledge to application.

title: Balassa-Samuelson in the Long Run: Qualitative Success, Quantitative Limits
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD)

detail.title: Balassa-Samuelson in the Long Run: Qualitative Success, Quantitative Limits
detail.abstract: I qualitatively and quantitatively revisit the Balassa-Samuelson (BS) mechanism in the long run. Traditional panel regression specifications without time fixed effects are fragile, but adding time fixed effects yields a stable, positive BS elasticity across samples and frequencies-evidence that the data support BS qualitatively on average across countries. Quantitatively, however, a standard multi-country trade model fed only by observed sectoral productivity cannot match country paths and delivers too small magnitudes. These failures persist with costly trade, multi-country, multi-sector settings, input-output linkages, and time-varying trade costs.

title: Activating Window of Opportunities for Healthy Planning: Reviewing Regulatory, Systems, Engagement, Capability and Policy Approaches
affiliations: , University of Bristol and King’s College London

detail.title: Activating Window of Opportunities for Healthy Planning: Reviewing Regulatory, Systems, Engagement, Capability and Policy Approaches
