detail.abstract: Population health promotion depends on determinants, requiring appreciation of different systems. Spatial planning can influence these determinants, yet integrating health in planning remains difficult. This paper outlines approaches in regulatory compliance, leverage points, participation, capability improvement and policy windows to identify where actions can be most effective. Each approach offers distinct strengths: consistency, certainty, systemic impact, engagement entry points, capacity building and strategic timing. No single approach is sufficient; a hybrid strategy is needed to navigate complexity and activate opportunities across contexts. This paper advances effective healthy planning as a dynamic process requiring adaptability, situational awareness and capability development.

title: FOMO Economics: External Reference-Dependence and Risk-Taking in Household Portfolios
affiliations: Alfred Lerner College of Business and Economics, The University of Delaware, Netanya Academic College and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: FOMO Economics: External Reference-Dependence and Risk-Taking in Household Portfolios
detail.abstract: Individual investors are sensitive to peer performance and particularly dislike "falling behind." We use unique granular data on transactions and holdings of retail investors to study portfolio adjustment in response to relative performance of their portfolios. We show that investor behavior is consistent with preferences over future wealth that are S-shaped around an external reference point provided by a salient market benchmark: if their portfolio lags the index they tend to increase the risky share of their portfolio, as well as purchase riskier securities, as characterized by high market beta, idiosyncratic volatility, and positive skewness. As the salience of the market index increases, investors become more sensitive to relative performance. The effect is asymmetric, more pronounced in bull market periods when investors might be most fearful of missing out on gains experienced by their peers, and does not reverse when individual portfolios are ahead of the market. Our evidence provides a novel perspective on the individual investors' demand for risky assets.

title: Asset Pricing with Supply Shocks
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School, , Cornell University and

detail.title: Asset Pricing with Supply Shocks
detail.abstract: Exploiting the 2016 SEC Tick Size Pilot as a randomized controlled trial, we find that a 1% exogenous and uninformed reduction in share repurchases lowers stock prices by 2.6%. Although treatment and control firms announced similar repurchase programs, treatment firms repurchased 22% fewer shares, a difference unexpected by both managers and investors. This reduction stems from an unanticipated conflict between the pilot and repurchase regulations. Because control stocks are unshocked, they allow us to control for price spillovers and identify a relative price multiplier. We further show that under a demand system, the relative price multiplier empirically approximates the own-price multiplier at the individual stock level. Finally, we find that investment advisors, mutual funds, and households absorb most of the supply shocks, followed by banks and other 13F institutions, while pension funds and insurance companies do not respond. The sizable uninformed price impact constrains managers' ability to repurchase undervalued equity and provides a new perspective on the long-run abnormal returns following repurchase announcements.

title: Substitutability In The Demand For Housing Over Small Distances
affiliations: George Mason University - Mercatus Center

detail.title: Substitutability In The Demand For Housing Over Small Distances
detail.abstract: Some pairs of residential locations are better substitutes for one another than others, perhaps even within two hundred meters' distance. As a result, rents and home prices can behave in ways that depart from the predictions of the most common urban economics models. The imperfect and varying substitutability between locations may arise due to preferences, information, or moving costs. Literatures in economics and complementary disciplines offer indirect evidence on the spatial substitutability of housing, homebuyers' housing search processes, and the information accessed by housing searchers. The available evidence suggests that spatial substitutability varies from place to place, is non-monotonic across space, and is endogenous to market conditions. Housing searchers vary widely, and their diversity can produce market outcomes that differ substantially from those predicted by models where all searchers are the same. Spatial substitutability has implications for policy debates around gentrification, market power, and zoning.

title: Crypto Expert Survey - Methodology
affiliations: IU International University of Applied Sciences

detail.title: Crypto Expert Survey - Methodology
detail.abstract: This paper documents the methodology of the Crypto Expert Survey, a harmonized quarterly expert survey that measures expectations and sentiment in the crypto sector across European countries. National partner institutions recruit expert panels and administer the survey locally, while IU International University of Applied Sciences aggregates and harmonizes the resulting data centrally. I describe the survey implementation, the core questionnaire, validation rules, and the construction of the CES headline indicators: the Crypto Business Climate Index, the Crypto Optimism Index, and Crypto Market Expectation Indices (BTC Price Expectation, BTC Volatility Expectation).

title: Winning Big, Swinging Wide: Electoral Competition and Ideological Extremism

detail.title: Winning Big, Swinging Wide: Electoral Competition and Ideological Extremism
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether greater electoral security is associated with individual legislators adopting more extreme positions in the U.S. House of Representatives. Building on George Stigler's (1972) theory that larger margins of victory can empower political parties to pursue more extreme policies, the analysis extends his framework to the individual level. Using panel data from the 95th to the 117th Congresses, election results from the MIT Election Lab (2024) are combined with modified Nokken-Poole ideology scores from Voteview (2025) to test whether representatives with greater vote shares exhibit more ideologically extreme roll call behavior. A linear fixed effects model with controls for party-by-Congress, district-byredistricting cycle, and individual legislators indicates that following the rise of the internet, higher vote shares are positively associated with ideological extremism. Robustness checks, including models accounting for unopposed elections and endogeneity concerns, reinforce this finding. These findings not only support Stigler's original theory but also suggest that the internet has lowered coordination costs for motivated voter subgroups, amplifying polarization among electorally secure legislators.

title: Designing an efficient reference rate: Lessons from SOFIA
affiliations: Reserve Bank of Australia, Reserve Bank of Australia, University of Melbourne - Department of Finance, University of Adelaide and University of Technology Sydney (UTS)

detail.title: Designing an efficient reference rate: Lessons from SOFIA
detail.abstract: We evaluate the informational efficiency of the Secured Overnight Funding Index Australia (SOFIA™), currently in its beta phase, and how design choices may impact the benchmark. We use a state-space model to separate time-varying noise in the benchmark from the underlying efficient rate and investigate the determinants of noise in the daily time series and at the transaction level. Related-party transactions, high market concentration, and low transaction volumes are associated with higher noise. Our modelling suggests that considering alternative methods for trimming the transactions used in calculating the benchmark, compared to the current approach, may enhance its informational efficiency and robustness. These results provide evidence on how to optimise the benchmark’s design. Indeed, the Australian Stock Exchange has already adjusted its SOFIA methodology to reflect most of these findings, in preparation for the potential transition of SOFIA from its beta phase to a live benchmark.

title: A Theory of Long-run Development with Capital
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) - Department of Economics and University of Manchester

detail.title: A Theory of Long-run Development with Capital
detail.abstract: This paper offers a unified framework for understanding long-run growth across the preindustrial, transitional, and industrial eras. We build a flexible growth model with three factors of production (land, capital and labor) and two distinct productivities which separately augment land/labor and capital/labor complementarities. The structure generates endogenously variable elasticities of substitution between inputs and can explain dynamic shifts in both factor income shares and aggregate output for an entire time series of aggregate data. When estimated on historical data from England and Wales, we show both theoretically and quantitatively that the model successfully reconciles multiple growth regimes.

title: AI Debris: Residual Risk and the Afterlife of Failed AI Systems

detail.title: AI Debris: Residual Risk and the Afterlife of Failed AI Systems
detail.abstract: AI governance frameworks primarily focus on risks during the development and deployment phases, implicitly treating system withdrawal as merely a technical shutdown. This paper argues that decommissioned AI systems generate residual risk-"AI debris"that persists after models are removed and continues to shape institutional behaviour, accountability, and trust. AI debris is defined as the post-withdrawal socio-technical residue of AI systems, including workflo w dependency, data contamination, capability displacement (deskilling), legitimacy erosion, and accountability breakdown. The paper develops a typology of debris domains and explains the mechanisms by which debris persists in institutional memory, path dependency, blame avoidance, and feedback effects within organisational data. To operationalise the concept, the paper proposes an evaluator-ready AI Debris Decommissioning Protocol (AIDP): a stepwise checklist specifying auditable evidence for freezing decision footprints, incident review, remediation, contestability, and postwithdrawal accountability assignment. A brief vignette of Amazon's discontinued hiring tool illustrates how algorithmic systems can institutionalise decision categories and screening heuristics that persist after rollback. The paper contributes a practical governance instrument for regulators, auditors, and organisations seeking to prevent "paper compliance," strengthen AI lifecycle governance, and improve institutional resilience in high-stakes decision environments.

title: Turning Polycrisis into Polytunity
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Turning Polycrisis into Polytunity

keywords: Fairy Tales of Western Development [Political Economy]

detail.abstract: In this UNDP expert commentary, Yuen Yuen Ang reframes today’s “polycrisis” as a “polytunity”: a rupture that can catalyze paradigm change in development thinking. She argues that prevailing industrial-colonial, machine-mode assumptions misread complex social systems as controllable mechanisms, encouraging one-size-fits-all reforms and Western end-state benchmarking. In place of this, Ang proposes an adaptive, inclusive and moral (AIM) political economy that treats development as non-linear coevolution, foregrounds power asymmetries, and builds “meta-institutions” that enable discovery. She then illustrates AIM through methods for mapping state–market coevolution and through the Unbundled Corruption Index, which distinguishes petty, grand, speed, and access corruption to decolonize measurement and target reforms.

title: Kinks and Gains from Credit Cycles
affiliations: University of Copenhagen - Department of Economics, Copenhagen Business School, University of Copenhagen and Catholic University of the Sacred Heart of Milan -  Department of Economics

detail.title: Kinks and Gains from Credit Cycles
detail.abstract: We examine the welfare cost of business cycles in a small open economy model with an occasionally binding collateral constraint. Aggregate uncertainty affects welfare through two opposing forces shaping households' value function: i) a loss reflecting the concavity of current utility, which stems from both prudence and the kink in debt determination; and ii) an offsetting force driven by precautionary saving, which shifts the distribution of future states away from severe episodes of financial tightness, as implied by the convexity of the continuation value. When the latter dominates, uncertainty is welfare-enhancing relative to the deterministic steady state. These fundamental properties are robust to the presence of pecuniary externalities, alternative timing assumptions for the collateral price, and to an environment in which the borrowing constraint does not bind in the steady state.

title: An Impossibility Theorem for Price-Based Risk Constraints
affiliations: BI Norwegian Business School

detail.title: An Impossibility Theorem for Price-Based Risk Constraints
detail.abstract: Price-based risk constraints map sampled transaction prices into measured risk and then into binding requirements. We prove a constructive local impossibility theorem: at reachable binding states with sufficiently strong amplification, no such rule can simultaneously satisfy three desirable properties. First, risk sensitivity: posted requirements increase at first order with the measured risk statistic. Second, liquidity continuity: prices and positions respond continuously to small shocks. Third, manipulation-proofness: no admissible finite-horizon round trip yields strictly positive expected profit. Unlike classic manipulation, the mechanism does not require large trades, large price moves, or making a slack constraint bind. A small trade can affect the prices used by the rule, tighten requirements, induce predictable forced selling, and then be reversed profitably. The result holds even with continuous trading between discrete measurement and reset dates, and it survives strategic responses by constrained investors. Manipulability is strongest when realized risk is low.

title: When Neighbors Stop Knocking: The Impact of Canada's 2025 Tourism Decline on U.S. Local Labor Markets
affiliations: Drexel University, York University - Faculty of Liberal Arts & Professional Studies and University of Quebec at Montreal (UQAM)

detail.title: When Neighbors Stop Knocking: The Impact of Canada's 2025 Tourism Decline on U.S. Local Labor Markets
detail.abstract: We provide the first systematic evidence on the labor market consequences of the 25% decline in Canadian visits to the United States in 2025. We combine smartphone foot-traffic data measuring Canadian visitor presence at the ZIP code × industry level with real-time establishment-level employment records. Using a difference-indifferences design, we find that establishments in highly exposed markets experienced employment declines of about 6%, implying a loss of 13,900 to 42,100 jobs. These effects are spatially concentrated and should be interpreted as lower bounds, as our analysis focuses on small and medium establishments and abstracts from spillover effects.

title: Pay or Prepare? How Tuition Shapes Student Effort in College Admissions
affiliations: University of Texas at San Antonio - College of Business - Department of Economics

detail.title: Pay or Prepare? How Tuition Shapes Student Effort in College Admissions
detail.abstract: In centralized college admissions systems, tuition differentiation influences not only application decisions but also students' incentives to invest in costly exam preparation prior to matching. This paper examines how tuition policies reshape pre-matching effort, equilibrium admission cutoffs, and welfare. Using administrative data and a nationally representative survey from the Turkish college admissions market, we document that students from higher socioeconomic backgrounds exert less preparation effort despite substantial returns to effort in terms of exam scores and admission probabilities. We develop and estimate a structural model in which students choose preparation effort while anticipating admission cutoffs and tuition payments under the Deferred Acceptance mechanism. Counterfactual simulations show that tuition payments and preparation effort are substitutes in expected utility. Welfare is non-monotonic in tuition generosity: eliminating subsidies induces excessive effort, whereas universal funding weakens incentives. A mixed funding regime mitigates congestion and maximizes expected welfare, raising student welfare by approximately $2,000 relative to a full-tuition benchmark.

title: Relationship Dynamics in the Federal Funds Market
affiliations: Independent, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Relationship Dynamics in the Federal Funds Market
detail.abstract: The federal funds market plays a central role in U.S. monetary policy implementation through its connection to the Effective Federal Funds Rate (EFFR), yet available transaction-level data do not identify the lenders of federal funds trades. We develop a matching procedure that links Fedwire Funds Service payments with borrowing reported on the FR 2420 Report on Selected Money Market Rates to recover the identities of the lenders of bilateral federal funds transactions. The resulting data identify lenders for approximately 95 percent of reported borrowing volume from January 2018 to November 2024. Using these data, we document that federal funds trading is concentrated in two segments: a dominant segment in which Federal Home Loan Banks lend primarily to foreign banking organizations and large domestic banks, and a smaller interbank segment primarily consisting of bankers' banks lending mainly to small and regional domestic banks. In both segments, trading is highly concentrated and relationship-based. Relationships are associated with larger and more stable borrowing volumes and modest differences in rates. We also examine how these patterns vary during recent funding stress episodes.

title: Institutional Mediation Model (IMM): A Three-Layer Governance Diagnostic for National Digital Missions

detail.title: Institutional Mediation Model (IMM): A Three-Layer Governance Diagnostic for National Digital Missions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Illustrative empirical data from survey of 720 farming households, Prayagraj district (2023), conducted as part of postgraduate research at SHUATS under institutional ethical supervision. Informed consent obtained from all participants.
declarations.funderStatement: Postgraduate research conducted under institutional supervision at SHUATS. No external funding received.

detail.abstract: This working paper introduces the Institutional Mediation Model (IMM), a governance diagnostic framework explaining why national digital reform missions systematically underperform when digital investments pass through unreformed institutional structures. The IMM proposes that digital investment must pass through three mediation layers — Governance, Human, and Community — each of which generates a Design-Reality Gap when structurally unreformed. The framework synthesises three established theoretical traditions: the Design-Reality Gap (Heeks 2002), institutional isomorphism (DiMaggio and Powell 1983), and street-level bureaucracy (Lipsky 1980). A critical theoretical extension is proposed: design-reality gaps at each layer are compounding rather than additive, meaning that sequential layer-by-layer reform produces persistently disappointing outcomes. The IMM is applied illustratively to two of India's major digital reform programmes — the Digital Agriculture Mission (2024–2028) and the National Education Policy 2020/NDEAR — drawing on original survey data from 720 smallholder farmers in Prayagraj district, Uttar Pradesh to demonstrate community layer dynamics in agricultural extension. The paper makes three original contributions: a named layered governance diagnostic for mission-level digital reform; an extension of the Design-Reality Gap framework from project-level to mission-level analysis; and a five-step diagnostic protocol for application by researchers and practitioners. The IMM is offered as a working framework for comment, empirical testing, cross-country application, and extension to healthcare (Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission), financial inclusion (PM Jan Dhan Yojana), and other national digital schemes.

title: The Pricing of Publicly Traded Private Credit Managers: An Exploratory Study of Market Performance and Event-Driven Returns
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The Pricing of Publicly Traded Private Credit Managers: An Exploratory Study of Market Performance and Event-Driven Returns
detail.abstract: This exploratory study investigates how public equity markets price publicly traded private credit managers, a rapidly growing segment of the financial system operating at the intersection of asset management, direct lending, and shadow banking. The private credit sector has expanded significantly in the post-Global Financial Crisis era, driven by regulatory changes affecting traditional banks and sustained investor demand for yield (Adrian, Ashcraft, & Cetorelli, 2013; Chernenko, Erel, & Prilmeier, 2022). Despite its growing systemic importance, relatively little academic work has examined the equity valuation of these firms. Using daily return data from January 2022 through February 2026 for a sample of eight firms, including pure-play private credit managers (Blue Owl Capital, Ares Management, Apollo Global Management, Blackstone, KKR, and TPG) and diversified financials with private credit exposure (Carlyle Group and Franklin Resources), this study examines return patterns, factor exposures, and stock price reactions to three key stress events. The findings reveal that pure-play private credit managers exhibit distinct return characteristics, with technology and financial sector exposures accounting for much of their apparent market sensitivity. After controlling for these factors, the average market beta of pure-play firms falls from 1.57 to 0.28. Event study results demonstrate that markets systematically distinguish between pure-play and diversified business models. During the Blackstone BREIT crisis of 2022, pure-play firms experienced significant negative abnormal returns averaging negative 5.64 percent, while diversified firms gained 3.03 percent on average. During the First Brands Group and Tricolor Holdings bankruptcies of 2025, pure-play firms gained 2.10 percent while diversified firms declined by 1.86 percent. During the Blue Owl OBDC II redemption modification of February 2026, pure-play firms declined by 8.64 percent on average, with significant contagion observed among competitors. All differences between groups are statistically significant at the one percent level. These findings contribute to the literature on financial intermediation and shadow banking while providing evidence for investors and regulators seeking to understand this rapidly growing sector.

title: Copyright's Jagged Frontier
affiliations: Emory University School of Law

detail.title: Copyright's Jagged Frontier

publicationDetails.detailsText: Duke Law Journal (forthcoming)

detail.abstract:
How should law respond to transformative technologies whose benefits are inseparable from their risks? This Article argues that the answer lies not in binary choices between permission and prohibition, but in what might be called zones of contingent permission: legal frameworks that allow deployment of new technologies while requiring measures to detect and prevent specific harms. The concept emerges from an unlikely source: the ongoing litigation over whether and when training generative AI models on copyrighted works constitutes infringement. 

Recent victories for Anthropic and Meta suggest AI training is fair use, but deeper analysis shows that will only sometimes be true. This Article explains why the boundary between permissible and infringing AI conduct will be jagged rather than smooth: the same computational process applied to a music model and a text model can produce dramatically different copyright risk, because memorization rates vary depending on a host of technical conditions and also because copyright’s threshold of substantial similarity that determines infringement is applied quite differently to some works compared to others.

That jagged frontier is only the beginning of the story. Drawing on Ronald Coase’s insight that legal rules are starting points for adaptation and negotiation rather than final allocations, this Article argues that the extensive literature on AI and copyright has focused almost exclusively on fair use while ignoring what comes next. AI companies that build systems to monitor and filter infringing outputs will not only reduce their legal exposure; they will create a deal point. The history of YouTube’s Content ID suggests that copyright safety infrastructure can become the foundation of a billion-dollar licensing industry benefiting developers, rights holders, and users alike.

title: The Effect of Disability Benefit Reform on the Mental Health of Older People in England
affiliations: University of York, University of York, University of York and University of York - Centre for Health Economics

detail.title: The Effect of Disability Benefit Reform on the Mental Health of Older People in England

detail.abstract: We estimate the effect of a disability benefit reform on older disabled people in England. The reform replaced Disability Living Allowance (DLA) with Personal Independence Payments (PIP), a benefit with tighter eligibility criteria. Most existing DLA claimants were required to be reassessed for PIP. We exploit the fact that people born before 8 April 1948 were exempt from reassessment, creating a sharp discontinuity in exposure by date of birth. We use this in a sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD), and find that the reform caused a significant worsening of mental health but did not reduce the probability of claiming disability benefits or total disability benefit payments. Our results provide evidence that the assessment process for disability benefit can have adverse health effects, even when benefits are not withdrawn.

title: Creative Machines: Neural Complementarity and the Organization of Human-AI Collaboration in Cultural Industries
affiliations: 'Gabriele d'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara, 'Gabriele d'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara, 'Gabriele d'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara, 'Gabriele d'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara, 'Gabriele d'Annunzio' University of Chieti-Pescara and

detail.title: Creative Machines: Neural Complementarity and the Organization of Human-AI Collaboration in Cultural Industries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None of the authorsw has a conflict of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not necessary for this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This paper received no funding.

detail.abstract: Can machines be creative? This paper addresses such question by developing a neural complementarity framework for understanding and organizing human-AI creative collaboration in cultural industries. We argue that human and AI creativity operate through fundamentally different mechanisms: humans excel at transformational creativity grounded in embodied cognition and contextual meaning-making; AI excels at combinatorial exploration and pattern recognition at scale. These differences are complementary rather than competitive, but optimal outcomes emerge only when organizational structures preserve conditions for distinctively human creative engagement. Drawing on experimental evidence showing that collaboration mode significantly affects outcomes, with AI as "sounding board" preserving human agency whereas AI as "ghostwriter" undermines it, we develop implications for organizational design, business models, labor markets, and governance. The framework suggests that creative value increasingly resides in human contributions that current AI architectures cannot replicate: contextual judgment, meaning-making, and the capacity to restructure conceptual spaces. We provide stakeholder-specific recommendations for creative industry managers, business strategists, workers, policymakers, and educators navigating AI-mediated transformation.

Exposure-Time Normalized Performance 
Strategy Evaluation Under Binding Exposure Constraints

detail.abstract: Standard risk-adjusted performance measures-Sharpe ratio, MAR ratio, information ratio-evaluate return per unit of risk but ignore how long capital is exposed to market risk. This paper formalizes exposure-time as a measurable input in strategy evaluation by defining the exposure fraction T e (proportion of trading days with an active position) and introducing exposure-normalized measures S* = S / T e and MAR* = MAR / T e. Under binding exposure constraints, the lower-T e strategy strictly expands the investor's feasible set (Proposition 1), and convex leverage costs prevent costless neutralization of exposure differences (Proposition 2). Empirical analysis using reconstructed S&P 500 annual returns (2000-2024) shows that a 200-day SMA timing strategy achieves lower Sharpe than buy-and-hold (0.19 vs. 0.28) but nearly identical S* (0.27 vs. 0.28) due to T e = 0.72. A Monte Carlo study across 2,000 simulated paths confirms that for this strategy pair and data generating process, exposure-normalized rankings reverse in 69.5% of simulations.

title: Granular Fiscal Risk and Tax-Base Concentration: Evidence from Macau's Gaming Industry
affiliations: City University of Macau, Bank of Korea and University of Macau

detail.title: Granular Fiscal Risk and Tax-Base Concentration: Evidence from Macau's Gaming Industry
detail.abstract: We document granular fiscal risk in the Macau Special Administrative Region of China: the non-diversifiable component of public-finance risk that arises when government revenues depend on a highly concentrated tax base. To quantify this exposure, we construct firm-level revenue residuals, decompose them into sector-wide and firm-specific components, and aggregate them using lagged Domar-style weights that reflect fiscal relevance. We examine how these shocks relate to macroeconomic and fiscal outcomes using static regressions, nonlinear specifications, and impulse responses estimated with Bayesian Vector Autoregressions and Local Projections. We find that sector-wide shocks are closely associated with movements in the mean of macro-fiscal outcomes. Firm-specific shocks, in contrast, are primarily linked to macroeconomic and fiscal volatility. These results indicate that tax-base concentration shapes not only the average macro-fiscal outcomes but also the underlying risk.

title: The Effect of Exchange Rate Volatility and Labor Market Rigidity on Export Growth
affiliations: University of Tsukuba and University of Tsukuba

detail.title: The Effect of Exchange Rate Volatility and Labor Market Rigidity on Export Growth
detail.abstract: The exchange rate is one of the most volatile macroeconomic price variables. Fluctuations in the exchange rate generate volatility in the profits of firms and reduce incentives for firms to enter the market or expand their capacity. In response to exchange rate volatility, firms can reduce labor costs to mitigate the negative impact by firing workers. However, rigidity in the labor market restricts a firm’s ability to implement this adjustment. These restrictions can amplify the negative effects of exchange rate volatility on economic outcomes. This study examines the interaction effects of exchange rate volatility and labor market rigidity on export growth using comprehensive panel data. To quantify the interaction effects of exchange rate volatility and labor market rigidity, we employ a panel fixed effects econometric model, which is analogous to the difference-indifferences approach. We construct a source-target-industry panel for 135 source countries, a maximum of 183 targets, and 17 industries over a span of 14 years from 2005 to 2018. Our results imply that in a country where labor market rigidity is one standard deviation higher, a one standard deviation increase in exchange rate volatility reduces export growth by 0.31 percentage points. In a subsample analysis, we find that the interaction between exchange rate volatility and labor market rigidity has a more pronounced negative impact on export growth in Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries compared to non-OECD countries. We also find that there is little treatment heterogeneity across industries.

title: Sports Betting, Lotteries, and State Revenues in the Post-PASPA Era
affiliations: West Virginia University, , University of Wisconsin - La Crosse, Florida Gulf Coast University and West Virginia University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Sports Betting, Lotteries, and State Revenues in the Post-PASPA Era
detail.abstract: State lotteries are a staple of state revenue for the 45 states that run them and are an important part of state public finance. Following the repeal of the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act (PASPA), 38 states, plus Washington, DC, began operating legal sports betting markets. It is unclear whether sports betting and lottery demand are substitutes, complements, or unrelated goods, but if the introduction of sports betting displaces expenditures from state lotteries to support sports gambling, state revenues could be severely impacted. Taking a cumulative revenue perspective, we combine monthly lottery revenue data for 18 states with sports betting data, and implement a difference-indifferences design, exploiting the staggered rollout of sports betting legalization following the repeal of PASPA. Our results show that sports betting does not impact overall monthly state lottery revenues and is robust across different specifications and sub-samples.

title: Harmonising Consensus: The (Geo)Political Economy of Standardisation in the AI Act
affiliations: University of Tartu

detail.title: Harmonising Consensus: The (Geo)Political Economy of Standardisation in the AI Act
detail.abstract: This paper examines the broader implications of current global (geo)political dynamics on AI standardisation and how, in turn, standardisation shapes those dynamics. Focusing on the European Union's AI Act, it argues that the Regulation's reliance on delegated technical standards embeds structural and context-dependent vulnerabilities that constrain its ability to project normative influence. Through insights from the political economy of standardisation, the paper explores the interactions between EU and non-EU aspirations and expectations from standards. It contrasts the EU, the US and China approaches and highlights the operational and normative frictions that arise in standard-setting. The findings show an important gap between the EU's regulatory ambitions and the realities of the global standardisation ecosystem, which ultimately raises questions about the long-term coherence and influence of the AI Act in shaping the global AI value chain.

detail.title: Sequencing Electrification Under Distribution Congestion

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on publicly available data, policy reports, and engineering literature. It does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental subjects. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Europe’s energy transition is entering a phase where electrification demand is accelerating across multiple sectors simultaneously, including electric mobility, digital infrastructure, building heating, and industrial processes. While policy discussions have largely focused on expanding renewable generation and strengthening transmission networks, emerging evidence suggests that the next operational constraint may increasingly appear at the distribution level.

Medium-voltage networks supplying urban clusters and industrial corridors are beginning to experience concentrated demand growth as multiple electrification pathways converge geographically. Under these conditions, substations may approach capacity thresholds within compressed timeframes, potentially triggering parallel reinforcement cycles across several locations.

This paper examines the structural dynamics behind this emerging distribution constraint and proposes a complementary operational framework for managing congestion during periods of rapid electrification. Rather than replacing infrastructure expansion, the framework introduces a sequencing approach that allows distribution system operators to utilise existing headroom more efficiently through controlled topology optimisation under strict engineering and regulatory constraints.

Using an illustrative urban distribution cluster scenario, the paper demonstrates how limited redistribution of load between adjacent substations may extend operational headroom while long-term reinforcement projects proceed. The analysis highlights how such sequencing mechanisms could help smooth capital deployment, reduce implementation bottlenecks, and improve investment timing under uncertain demand trajectories.

The findings suggest that as electrification accelerates across Europe, the pace of the energy transition may increasingly depend not only on how much infrastructure is built, but on how intelligently distribution capacity expansion is sequenced.

title: Taxonomy of Civilian Political Leadership and Nigeria's Postmilitary Redemocratization, 1999-2023
affiliations: Rhema Univeristy, Nigeria.

detail.title: Taxonomy of Civilian Political Leadership and Nigeria's Postmilitary Redemocratization, 1999-2023
detail.abstract: This study was designed to explore a brand of leadership where civilians control the machinery of a government, including the authority to set military priorities, allocate resources, and to oversee the armed forces and its relationship with redemocratization, after a period of dedemocratization. Dedemocratization is often a function of military intervention in civilian democratic leadership. Dedemocratization involves the dismantling of democratic structures like political parties, the constitution and other relevant institutions for a democratic polity. The wave of dedemocratization in Nigeria began with the January 15, 1966 military coup and the subsequent July, 1966 counter military coup. There was a sign of redemocratization in 1979 which was short-lived, until the full process of redemocratization began in 1999. Redemocratization is the process by which a country journeys from an authoritarian regime back to a democratic one. It involves the re-establishment or establishment of political rights, institutions, and civil liberties, like free and fair elections, often following a period of military rule. Contrary to military leadership which is generally characterized by impunity, civilian political leadership is a function of certain key elements such as civilian control of the military. Civilian control of the military or civilian supremacy simply means the control over the armed forces by the civilian authority, as well as making the final decision on a country's defense policies, the use of troops and military budgets. Civilian political leadership in terms of democratization or redemocratization is characterized by one of its finest elements of representation. Representation is a combination of public deliberation and consensus building within parliament, as well as the engagement of citizens on matters of public policy. This idea of representation strives best through the electoral process. This is obvious because the electoral process describes the method by which an individual is elected to public office, and also suggests taking and counting of votes. This also emphasizes the importance of the political party in the process of democratization or redemocratization in the polity and democratic consolidation. The hallmark of democratic consolidation involves improving the architecture of governance so as to pave the way of good governance. Good governance based on the principles of constitutional democracy, the rule of law, separation of powers, enhances the common good and promotes equitable, human, social, political and economic society. The qualitative exploratory research design was adopted in this investigation and the result showed significant positive relationship between civilian political leadership and redemocratization. The study was never exhaustive due to lack of relevant current literature in these areas and research funding. Further study could examine the relationship between civilian political leadership and democratic accountability as a measure of reducing the disease of corruption in Nigeria. This investigation recommends that recruitment into the armed forces, police, and other paramilitary agencies needs to be more thoroughly done to avoid the dangers of bringing in terrorists' agents at the detriment of the people.

title: Capacity Constraints, Encounter Frequency, and the Paradox of Tightening
affiliations: NTNU Business School

detail.title: Capacity Constraints, Encounter Frequency, and the Paradox of Tightening
detail.abstract: I study enforcement systems that observe regulated activity through discrete administrative encounters (filings, inspections, audits) under binding screening capacity. When agents can choose how to partition a fixed activity volume across encounters, per-encounter procedural burdens induce consolidation into fewer and larger encounters. If screening resources are allocated at the encounter level and scale sublinearly with encounter scope, detectability declines with encounter size. In that case, tightening procedural requirements can reduce equilibrium detection by triggering discrete reductions in encounter frequency, generating a non-monotonic relationship between stringency and effective enforcement. The analysis delivers comparative statics for consolidation thresholds and shows how design features that scale screening with encounter size-through sampling, automation, or size-contingent escalation-eliminate the paradox channel by preserving screening intensity per unit.

title: Two Central Bank Instruments for Money Velocity and Capital Mobility

detail.title: Two Central Bank Instruments for Money Velocity and Capital Mobility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The Federal Reserve has effectively one instrument — the federal funds rate — and no instrument for money velocity. Carrying costs on idle money have been proposed since Gesell (1916) and formalized by Buiter (2003, 2009), but every implementation failed because holders escaped through uncharged exit channels. A companion paper (Demyanov 2026) constructs a two-perimeter architecture that prices every recognized position and transition, and — jointly with Demyanov (2026c) for fixed nominal claims — establishes no lower-burden path through recognized positions. This paper analyzes the monetary policy implications of two instruments within that architecture: a carrying cost δ on checking-account balances and on non-exempt registered assets held on checking-account terms — a proposed enforceable velocity instrument — and a carrying cost ρ on cross-border receivables — a proposed continuously adjustable capital flow instrument. Without ρ, the Fed lacks an independent instrument on the cross-border receivables margin; without δ, the velocity of existing domestic money remains uncontrolled. Together with the federal funds rate and the reserve ratio θ, the toolkit {i, θ, δ, ρ} supplies four independently adjustable instruments operating on four distinct margins: the price of new credit, the banking system stability floor, the velocity of existing money, and the domestic-vs-international allocation of capital. The instruments do not require observing all economic activity; they price positions administered within formal infrastructure — banks, registries, custodians — that agents continue to choose because it provides enforceable property rights, payment services, and legal recourse. Whether these margins are fully orthogonal, and the associated welfare gains, remain questions for formal general equilibrium analysis. For fixed nominal claims, the no-evasion result is joint with Demyanov (2026c).

detail.abstract: Climate-induced internal migration is increasingly reshaping urban vulnerability in Bangladesh, yet governance responses remain fragmented and largely emergency-driven. This study examines how community-structured interventions influence health outcomes, social integration, and adaptive capacity among climate-displaced populations in high-density urban settlements. Drawing on field-based evidence from ward-level interventions in Chattogram, the research analyzes tuberculosis detection, vector-borne disease prevention, maternal health engagement, and community trust-building mechanisms implemented through decentralized local facilitation models. Findings indicate that proactive household screening, structured follow-up systems, and community health mediation significantly improved early health-seeking behavior, accelerated tuberculosis diagnosis and treatment adherence, reduced dengue and diarrheal incidence through environmental management, and increased antenatal engagement in high-risk clusters. Beyond clinical outcomes, the interventions strengthened social cohesion and reduced service-access barriers among migrant households. The study argues that climate migration should be reframed from a humanitarian crisis response to a managed urban adaptation process supported by locally embedded governance structures. It proposes a multi-level Climate Migration Governance Framework integrating cross-ministerial coordination, citylevel institutionalization, climate-health integration, and blended financing mechanisms. By demonstrating how community-led facilitation can operationalize adaptation at scale, the paper contributes to emerging scholarship on climate mobility, urban resilience, and locally led adaptation in the Global South.

title: Regulatory Crowding-out under Capacity Constraints: Evidence from Multi-task Environmental Enforcement
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE), National University of Singapore (NUS) and

detail.title: Regulatory Crowding-out under Capacity Constraints: Evidence from Multi-task Environmental Enforcement
detail.abstract: Governments regulate multiple activities, but enforcement capacity is limited. This paper examines how demand in one regulatory domain crowds out enforcement in others. We use seasonal enforcement of agricultural open burning in China as an exogenous demand shock, leveraging county variation in crop maturity and planting patterns. Using administrative penalty records, we show that environmental inspectors reallocate attention away from industrial facilities during harvest windows, causing a 30% decline in industrial environmental penalties and a 6.3% increase in pollutant emissions at peak harvest. Effects are larger where regulatory capacity is tighter. Surveillance technology that lowers monitoring costs mitigates these distortions.

title: Market Responses to a VIX Shock *
affiliations: University of Vienna - Department of Statistics and Operations Research, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam and University of Copenhagen

detail.title: Market Responses to a VIX Shock *
detail.abstract: Implied variance (VIX) shocks can be caused by either a perceived higher expected future realized variance or an increase in the variance risk pre mium. We analyze thirty billion NASDAQ order book messages for equity and governmentbond exchangetraded funds to delineate how the market re sponds to shocks in either of these two components. We find that investors actively sell equities and buy government bonds on largely unchanged liq uidity in response to an elevated price of variance risk, e.g., due to height ened crashrisk probabilities. The response to an expected realized variance shock is active buying of equities on worse liquidity. This pattern is likely to be caused by an information shock.

title: Loss-aware Point Forecasts for Realised Variance
affiliations: University of Bristol Business School

detail.title: Loss-aware Point Forecasts for Realised Variance
detail.abstract: This paper develops a decision-theoretic framework for point forecasting positive risk measures under relative loss functions. We study a class of scale-free losses that includes absolute and squared percentage errors and derive the corresponding optimal forecasts for log-transformed realised variance models. The optimal forecast is obtained by exponentiating the conditional mean and applying a loss-dependent adjustment that reflects conditional uncertainty and the distribution of the forecast error. Closed-form expressions are provided for conditional Gaussian, Laplace, and logistic errors, allowing straightforward implementation with standard realised variance models. An empirical application to daily, weekly, and monthly realized variance forecasts for a panel of exchange-traded funds uses rolling model specifications and evaluates accuracy under relative loss. Loss-optimal forecasts consistently outperform conventional conditional-expectation-based forecasts, with economically and statistically significant efficiency gains that increase with the curvature of the loss function and the forecast horizon. The results show that forecast construction should be aligned with the decision objective and that accounting for conditional risk uncertainty can materially improve forecast accuracy without modifying the underlying model.

title: Declining Business Dynamism: The Heterogeneous Role of Market Power *
affiliations: University of Tartu - Faculty of Economics and Business Administration

detail.title: Declining Business Dynamism: The Heterogeneous Role of Market Power *
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the evolution of business dynamism in Estonia, focusing on job reallocation. Consistent with trends in other advanced economies, job reallocation rates have declined. Contrary to patterns observed elsewhere in Europe, however, the dispersion of productivity shocks in Estonia has increased since 2013-2015, indicating that reduced dynamism cannot be attributed to weaker productivity-enhancing activities. Rather, the responsiveness of employment growth to productivity shocks has diminished. We examine the role of market power in shaping these dynamics. While markups and labor markdowns reduce the responsiveness employment to productivity shocks in most sectors, there is heterogeneity in the way market power affects this responsiveness. In firms that use rents to earn economic profits, markups reduce the pass-through of productivity shocks to employment more compared to firms that use rents to cover fixed costs. Moreover, firms with higher share of fixed costs in the revenue exhibit higher job reallocation rates, suggesting that firms that use rents to cover fixed costs are dynamic. A novel one-step procedure, which extends the two-step proxy methods, for estimating production functions allows for imperfections in output and labor markets.

detail.abstract:
This inaugural Global Fintech Industry Association Study provides valuable data and insights into the approaches and practices of the global community of Digital Financial Services (DFS)/fintech industry associations. The findings from this study aim to help industry associations, policymakers, regulators, market participants, and the development community better understand the work of industry associations.  

Drawing from findings of an online survey of 65 industry associations in 48 jurisdictions, and in-depth interviews conducted with selected industry associations, the study discusses global approaches adopted by industry associations as well as lessons learned and good practices.  

It can be used both as reference material and a tool to strengthen the operations of fintech industry associations, especially those which are nascent. For more established industry associations, this research provides new insights into benchmarking and surfaces commonalities and learnings across diverse fintech markets. 

The research was conducted by the CCAF, working closely with the Alliance of Digital Finance and Fintech Associations (AllianceDFA), with the support of the Gates Foundation.

title: Bank of U.S. Redux

detail.title: Bank of U.S. Redux
detail.abstract: Revisiting the Bank of U.S., this paper explores the biggest depository failure on record in December 1930. A topic of debate, the institution's demise is attributed here to an overexpansion that included five banks purchased at peak prices in the sixteen months through May 1929. Spurred by the McFadden Act (1927), the Bank of U.S. was the worst offender in a wave of consolidation conspicuous for its use of security affiliates, which provided the vehicle for nefarious dealings that not only rendered it untouchable in a merger context but also raised the prospect that toxic assets resided in other banks.

title: Anticipating State Action: Risk Perceptions and Consumption under Immigration Enforcement
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago and University of Glasgow

detail.title: Anticipating State Action: Risk Perceptions and Consumption under Immigration Enforcement
detail.abstract: Immigration enforcement affects millions of individuals who make daily economic decisions under uncertainty about state action. Using data from 2014 to 2018, we study how households learn about and respond to enforcement risk by combining daily bank account transaction data with arrest-level records of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations. We document that enforcement follows predictable weekday patterns and that communities with large immigrant populations have learned them: Consumption is depressed not only on days when enforcement occurs, but also on the same weekday of other weeks-when no enforcement occurs-and rebounds in between, indicating that behavior tracks beliefs about enforcement risk, not just realized enforcement. Instrumenting for beliefs using the learnable structure of enforcement, we find that a 10 percentage point increase in perceived enforcement probability reduces Hispanic foreign-born consumption by approximately 5 percent. A structural model with Bayesian learning and pent-up demand reveals that roughly half of the immediate consumption decline is recovered through subsequent rebound; the rest is permanently foregone. Eliminating enforcement risk entirely would increase Hispanic foreign-born consumption by 3.6 percent, but when enforcement ceases, only 42 percent of these gains materialize within the first year-the remaining losses reflect learning frictions: even after state action stops, beliefs must still adjust.

title: Move Fast and Break Everything: Crypto, Democrats and Deregulation
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Boston - Department of Political Science, University of Massachusetts Boston, Johns Hopkins University and University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) (Formerly University of Texas-Pan American)

detail.title: Move Fast and Break Everything: Crypto, Democrats and Deregulation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series No. 245
publicationDetails.journalName: Institute for New Economic Thinking Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: In November, 2022, the giant cryptocurrency exchange FTX filed for bankruptcy. The financial fallout from that event, including two bank failures, made crypto politically radioactive. Yet less than three years later, crypto, like Donald Trump himself, staged a triumphant Second Coming, as the President signed into law the so-called "GENIUS Act" - short for Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins. Analysts have traced the industry's phoenix-like resurrection, showing how key crypto billionaires and companies aligned with Trump early in the 2024 campaign, transforming him from a skeptic into a political champion. But the flip side of the story is much less discussed: how support for crypto has grown among Democrats. This paper analyzes voting by House Democrats on the GENIUS and Clarity Acts, in the context of the campaign for sweeping financial deregulation mounted by both crypto and traditional finance. The implications of a growing race to the bottom in financial regulation and emerging challenges in cybersecurity receive attention.

title: Cracking Vicious Involution through a Social Operation Cost Anchoring Mechanism: Theoretical and Practical Explorations Based on Institutional Economics of Human Nature
affiliations: and Soochow University

detail.title: Cracking Vicious Involution through a Social Operation Cost Anchoring Mechanism: Theoretical and Practical Explorations Based on Institutional Economics of Human Nature
detail.abstract: The essence of current vicious involution lies in institutional disorder driven by myopic human nature, which induces market entities to engage in "bottom-line competition" under specific contexts. Enterprises prioritize shifting public costs such as social security and compliance to pursue immediate interests, rather than investing in high-risk, long-cycle innovation. Traditional theories and regulatory tools, which overlook the dialectical nature and contextual dependence of "myopic human nature," struggle to fundamentally address this dilemma. Based on the "Axiom of Myopic Human Nature" in institutional economics of human nature—incorporating contextual moderating variables such as economic cycles, industry risks, enterprise scale, and regional differences, supplemented by cross-regional and cross-cycle dynamic calibration logic—this paper constructs a "social operation cost anchoring mechanism." Through a three-dimensional quantitative measurement framework of "rigidity + flexibility + public sharing" (optimizing the sharing model with reference to Germany’s dual-system vocational education and adding a regional gradient adaptation plan), real-time incentive and constraint design, and regular expiration calibration, the mechanism deepens the dialogue with Schumpeter’s theory of "creative destruction." Employing scenario simulations of three industries—photovoltaic (manufacturing), food delivery platforms (service), and AI (digital economy)—with additional scenario-specific adaptation designs for AI, and combining survey data from manufacturing enterprises across the Yangtze River Delta, Pearl River Delta, and Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei regions as well as experiences from Germany’s dual-system, this study systematically compares the mechanism with traditional tools and international models. The results indicate that the mechanism can adapt to different contexts and industry characteristics, guiding competition from "bottom-line undercutting" to "innovative competition" and achieving the triple goals of "national stability, stable residents’ income, and smooth social production." Meanwhile, by constructing a "cost anchoring-innovation performance" dynamic evaluation system, the study quantitatively verifies the mechanism’s driving effect on innovation, making it a core achievement of institutional economics of human nature in connecting theoretical research with practical governance.

title: Climate Extremes and Inflation: Evidence from Italian Regional Data
affiliations: Bank of Italy

detail.title: Climate Extremes and Inflation: Evidence from Italian Regional Data

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 988
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper empirically investigates the impact of climate extremes on inflation, focusing on Italy and providing complementary evidence for the euro area. Using Italian regional data (NUTS2), which better capture the localized nature of climate extremes, it finds that extremely high temperatures generally exert downward pressure on inflation, whereas extremely low temperatures have a pronounced positive effect, mainly driven by energy price dynamics. Extreme precipitation is associated with decreases in energy prices. These findings highlight the need for central banks to incorporate climate-related shocks into their inflation assessments and policy frameworks.

title: Reaching Wide through Small Screens: The Impact of a Banca d’Italia Financial Education TV Campaign
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Reaching Wide through Small Screens: The Impact of a Banca d’Italia Financial Education TV Campaign

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 990
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Financial literacy is essential for personal and collective well-being yet remains low among adults worldwide, and traditional education programs often struggle to engage their audience. We explore a broader-reaching approach: delivering financial education through mass media. Using a randomized survey experiment with about 1,000 individuals, we evaluate the impact of a television campaign launched in 2023 by Banca d’Italia and the public broadcaster Rai, which covered various financial topics across multiple TV formats. Our findings show significant improvements in financial knowledge, particularly among women, individuals with lower financial literacy, and non-investors. The campaign also raised interest in financial topics and awareness of investment diversification. With approximately 7 million viewers in 2024, its potential impact is substantial. From a policy perspective, short-format financial education on television and social media constitutes a scalable, cost-effective complement to existing initiatives. While our findings are robust, they only capture short-term effects; further research is needed to assess long-term impact.

title: HawkesRank: Event-Driven Centrality for Real-Time Importance Ranking
affiliations: Risks-X, Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech), Southern University of Science and Technology and Southern University of Science and Technology

detail.title: HawkesRank: Event-Driven Centrality for Real-Time Importance Ranking

publicationDetails.detailsText: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper No. 26-28
publicationDetails.journalName: Swiss Finance Institute Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Quantifying influence in networks is important across science, economics, and public health, yet widely used centrality measures remain limited: they rely on static representations, heuristic network constructions, and purely endogenous notions of importance, while offering little semantic connection to observable activity. We introduce HawkesRank, a dynamic framework grounded in multivariate Hawkes point processes that models exogenous drivers (intrinsic contributions) and endogenous amplification (self-and cross-excitation). This yields a principled, empirically calibrated, and adaptive importance measure. Classical indices such as Katz centrality and PageRank emerge as mean-field limits of the framework, clarifying both their validity and their limitations. Unlike static averages, HawkesRank measures importance through instantaneous event intensities, enabling prediction, transparent endo-exo decomposition, and adaptability to shocks. Using both simulations and empirical analysis of emotion dynamics in online communication platforms, we show that HawkesRank closely tracks system activity and consistently outperforms static centrality metrics.

title: Ten Years on: has Italy’s Inner Areas Strategy Paid Off?
affiliations: Bank of Italy

detail.title: Ten Years on: has Italy’s Inner Areas Strategy Paid Off?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 992
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the impact of Italy’s National Strategy for Inner Areas (SNAI), a place-based policy launched in 2014 to counteract demographic and economic decline in peripheral areas. Using a staggered difference-in-differences approach on detailed municipal-level data, we find no evidence of population growth, consistent with the typically long timeframe required for demographic changes to manifest. In contrast, we observe a significant increase in local business density in treated municipalities, with no corresponding effects on employment and housing prices. Notably, municipalities with higher administrative capacity are more successful in attracting funding and exhibit stronger positive impacts, highlighting the critical role of governance quality in shaping policy outcomes. Geographical disparities emerge, with stronger economic effects observed in Central and Northern Italy.

title: Comparative Local Government Law in Motion: How Different Local Government Law Regimes Affect Global Cities’ Bike Share Plans
affiliations: Northwestern University - Pritzker School of Law and Northwestern University School of Law

detail.title: Comparative Local Government Law in Motion: How Different Local Government Law Regimes Affect Global Cities’ Bike Share Plans

publicationDetails.detailsText: 42 Fordham Urban Law Journal 123 (2015)
Northwestern Public Law Research Paper No. 15-52
publicationDetails.journalName: Northwestern University Pritzker School of Law, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: At the heart of the contemporary study of comparative local government law lies a paradox. On the one hand, the discipline relies on an assumption that there is a great deal of similarity between different cities across the world—an assumption evinced by adjectives such as “global,” “international,” or “world” that scholars routinely affix to the cities they compare. If no minimal baseline of commonality is assumed, the whole exercise becomes futile. What is the point of comparing things that have nothing in common? On the other hand, what can be more local—as opposed to “global” or “international”—than local government law? The local is in the name, and for good reason. Local government law structures the smallest-scale political institutions, those that are the closest to the specific community. Thus inevitably this body of law reflects the community’s particular culture and politics. Much of local government law is dedicated to the regulation of space: local government law’s scope of interest, indeed its job, is parochial by definition. This Article suggests and pursues one method for tackling this paradox presented by a field of law dedicated to the global attributes of the local (or the local attributes of the global). The Article explores one common, “global,” policy adopted by many cities despite the particular, parochial nature of their local government law regimes. The Article seeks to figure out how the particularities of the local government legal system affect—or do not affect—a policy the city imports from elsewhere.

title: Survey-Based Daily Estimates of Inflation Expectations and Risk Premia in the Euro Area
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy - Research Department

detail.title: Survey-Based Daily Estimates of Inflation Expectations and Risk Premia in the Euro Area

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 991
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In this research note, we develop real-time, daily estimates of survey-based inflation expectations and inflation risk premia for the euro area using a simple, nearly model-free approach. We first estimate daily inflation expectations by projecting low-frequency survey measures onto a small set of daily financial variables. We then compute daily inflation risk premia as the difference between inflation-linked swap (ILS) forward rates and the estimated survey-based expectations. The resulting daily estimates provide timely insights for conjunctural analysis and monetary policy, offering a useful complement to measures derived from dynamic term structure models.

title: We've Got You Covered: Firms' Political Stances on Abortion and Labor Market Sorting
affiliations: Indeed.com, Indeed.com, University of Southern California, Indeed Hiring Lab, Cornell  University,  Ithaca,  New  York and

detail.title: We've Got You Covered: Firms' Political Stances on Abortion and Labor Market Sorting

publicationDetails.detailsText: NBER Working Paper No. w34948
publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Amidst rising political polarization, firms engage more frequently with political issues through public statements and policies. This paper examines how firms' stances on polarizing issues impact worker sorting, leveraging announcements from hundreds of employers following the Supreme Court's ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson, overturning federal abortion rights. We introduce a methodology to uncover labor market competitors for each announcing firm based on job seekers' revealed preferences. While announcing firms received more applications from job seekers, particularly in Democratic-leaning states and female-dominated jobs where abortion was outlawed, current employees began searching for jobs elsewhere as employee satisfaction declined, particularly among male-dominated jobs. Smaller companies with less-established reputations experienced the largest effects. When deciding whether to take a sociopolitical stance, firms face a complicated trade-off: attracting culturally-aligned workers at the expense of alienating current ones.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: The Emperor Has No Cash Flows: Integrating Cash Flow Dynamics into Total Portfolio Approach
affiliations: Independant and Deutsche Bank Research

detail.title: The Emperor Has No Cash Flows: Integrating Cash Flow Dynamics into Total Portfolio Approach
detail.abstract: The total portfolio approach (TPA) promises to deliver sustainably higher returns by treating public and private assets on equal footing. First-generation TPA implementations naturally extended factor models as the unifying framework. However, private fund commitments introduce state variables that are orthogonal to factor exposures. Specifically, commitment-based investing creates cash flow dynamics, illiquidity by design, and operational requirements that factor loadings cannot represent. This paper argues that while factor models remain valuable for economic exposure analysis, they create analytical blind spots when applied to private market allocation decisions. Cash flow models address the critical questions factor frameworks were not designed to answer: commitment pacing, liquidity management, and allocation sizing. Sophisticated investors already use both approaches in complementary ways.

title: Yield Compression and Macroeconomic Drivers in Dubai Residential Market (2021-2025)

detail.title: Yield Compression and Macroeconomic Drivers in Dubai Residential Market (2021-2025)
detail.abstract: This paper examines the structural drivers of residential rental yield dynamics in Dubai during the post-pandemic expansionary cycle from 2021 to 2025. Using a dataset constructed from over 1.5 million residential transactions sourced from the Dubai Land Department, the study evaluates whether observed yield compression is primarily driven by capital value appreciation or by changes in the cost of capital, proxied by the one-year Emirates Interbank Offered Rate (EIBOR). Employing a log-log multiple linear regression framework, the analysis finds strong evidence that rising sale prices are the dominant determinant of declining rental yields, while interest rates play a secondary and statistically weaker role. The findings contribute to the literature on emerging-market housing finance by demonstrating that Dubai's residential market operates primarily as a capital-driven, rather than credit-driven, system, with important implications for investors and policymakers.

detail.abstract: This article examines how people perceive the fairness of carbon taxes when distributional outcomes are unequal. While fairness perceptions are known to be crucial for public support of carbon taxation, the mechanisms underlying it remain insufficiently understood. Using a factorial survey experiment with 770 Swiss citizens, we study how inequality aversion affects fairness perceptions, distinguishing between aversion to self-centred inequality and aversion to inequality in society. We find that fairness perceptions are strongly driven by the former: individuals who anticipate benefiting from a carbon tax are significantly more likely to perceive it as fair. At the same time, perceived fairness declines when individuals find themselves better off than others, indicating an aversion to relative advantage. Being worse off than others also reduces perceived fairness, although less consistently. Concerns about unequal outcomes in society play a more limited role and are politically conditioned: right-leaning respondents view unequal outcomes as less fair, whereas left-leaning respondents accept inequality when it disadvantages high emitters. Importantly, these patterns are largely independent of the specific policy sector in which the tax is applied. These findings show that fairness perceptions are shaped less by abstract redistribution principles than by relational comparisons and ideological interpretation. Carbon taxes are therefore more likely to be perceived as fair when distributional outcomes minimise salient disparities in net outcomes and can be credibly justified across the political spectrum.

detail.abstract: In 1979, less than 30 per cent of full-time university students in Canada worked for pay during the academic term. By 2000 this had risen to 45 per cent. We find that no economic variable other than tuition fees-which can account for half of the rise-can explain this increase. detail.abstract: Holdings-based factor attribution routinely applies a multi-factor risk model to a problem it was not designed to solve. Both failures are structural, not statistical. Observable attribution pathologies (e.g., highly correlated factor and specific contributions) are their predictable consequences.

detail.abstract:
Medium and low-voltage networks across Europe were not designed for the combined effects of synchronised high-power EV charging and sustained electricity demand growth from data centres and AI-related workloads. In dense urban environments where a substantial share of residents lack private parking and depend on shared or public charging infrastructure, these pressures compress local utilisation margins and heighten sensitivity to reinforcement timing.

Drawing on distribution network ageing data, grid investment requirements, and simulation-based evidence on transformer stress dynamics, this paper defines an emerging “reinforcement gap”: a structural misalignment between electrification adoption velocity and distribution reinforcement cycles. The resulting risk is not immediate systemic failure, but cumulative infrastructure friction expressed through accelerated asset ageing, connection delays, and uneven deployment feasibility across metropolitan districts.

Comparative acceleration pathways demonstrate that compressed electrification timelines amplify coordination challenges between infrastructure expansion and demand growth. Aligning electrification ambition with distribution reality will therefore require spatially informed deployment strategies, improved grid headroom transparency, and stronger coordination between policy frameworks, distribution system operators, and charging infrastructure providers.

Electrification at scale remains technically achievable. Its durability will depend on whether infrastructure pacing is synchronised with policy momentum in high-density urban systems.

detail.abstract: This paper revisits the relatively less talked about but yet vehemently argued debate in Indian agriculture compared to earlier, concerning the relationship between farm size and productivity. It then extends the analysis to related dimensions such as profitability and labour use across different farm-size categories so as to through light of the quality of life of the farmers. Using plot-level data from the Cost of Cultivation Surveys for 2021-22, conducted by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare, Government of India, the study examines these relationships for six major crops across nine key crop producing states representing the diverse agroclimatic regions in the country. The findings indicate a mild positive association between farm size and productivity, much in contrast to the earlier prevailing thought. Next, pronounced regional and crop-specific variations constrain the possibility of drawing uniform or generalisable conclusions regarding the farm size-productivity relationship in India.
