detail.abstract: Complex environments require leaders to make quick decisions that often lead to the conflation of decision-making and judgment (Tichy & Bennis, 2007). This paper demonstrates that these terms are separate by showing that decision-making is a momentary action, and judgment emerges as a developmental capacity expressed over time (Tichy & Bennis, 2007; Useem, 2010). Viewing judgment through the lens of complexity (Boulton et al., 2015; Wheatley, 2006), this paper further argues that judgment is not simply a skill, but instead is a capacity developed over time through enhancing sensemaking (Ancona, 2012), dialogue (Bohm, 2004), and suspension (Isaacs, 1999). Together, these capacities work together to surface biases and raise awareness of competing interpretations, all while holding tensions long enough for judgment to emerge. By distinguishing judgment from decision-making and showing how sensemaking, dialogue, and suspension support the development of judgment, this paper demonstrates that effective leadership under complexity depends less on the speed of decisions and more on cultivating judgment over time.

detail.abstract: Responsible artificial intelligence (RAI) is increasingly advocated as a design principle for socially beneficial innovation, yet whether RAI orientation creates tangible value in entrepreneurial finance remains unclear. Drawing on signal theory, we examine how RAI orientation affects investor syndication in healthcare AI ventures and how this relationship is contingent on technology, institutional, and ecosystem contexts. Analysing 1,123 investment deals in healthcare AI/ML clinical software ventures sourced from a leading private capital market database, we employ a two-way fixed-effects framework with sub-region and year fixed effects. We find that RAI orientation is positively associated with investor syndication (β = 0.191, p < 0.05), supporting its role as a credibility-enhancing signal under information asymmetry. However, this baseline effect is moderated by three contextual boundaries. First, generative AI capability substitutes for the RAI signal, reducing its value (β =-0.402, p < 0.01). Second, developed-market institutions crowd out the RAI signal (β =-0.215, p < 0.01), consistent with institutional substitution. Third, location in a US technology hub amplifies the RAI signal (β = 0.278, p < 0.01), reflecting ecosystem-level certification. Marginal effect analysis reveals that the RAI signal is most valued in emerging-market, non-generative-AI contexts (+0.191) and in technology hub ecosystems (+0.253), but is redundant in developed non-hub settings (-0.024, n.s.) and penalised in generative AI ventures (-0.211). These findings contribute to the socially responsible AI ecosystems literature by demonstrating that investor responses to RAI are not universal but are shaped by the socio-technical and institutional environment in which ventures operate.

detail.abstract: Projecting the effects of proposed policy reforms is challenging because no outcome data exist for regulations that governments have not yet implemented. We propose an ex ante deep learning framework that can project effects of proposed reforms by mapping outcomes observed under past regulations onto the legal criteria of proposed future policies (i.e., by “relabeling”). We apply this framework to study changes in jurisdiction of the US Clean Water Act (CWA). We compare our ex ante deep learning projection of jurisdiction under the Supreme Court’s Sackett decision against widely used projections from domain experts. Ex ante machine learning generates exceptional performance improvements over the leading domain expert model that the US Environmental Protection Agency currently uses, with 65 times more accurate identification of jurisdictional sites. We also develop an ex post deep learning model trained with data after policy implementation. Ex post deep learning performs best. Sackett deregulates one-third of all previously regulated US waters, particularly floodplains and pristine fish habitats, totaling 700,000 deregulated stream miles and 17 million deregulated wetland acres. Deep learning can effectively project consequences of far-reaching regulatory reforms before they are implemented, when projections are both most uncertain and most useful.
